articles.title: My password generator used crypto.getRandomValues and was still wrong 15% of the time
articles.description: My site has a small client-side password generator. It has a length slider, four checkboxes (A–Z,...
articles.body_html:
My site has a small client-side password generator. It has a length slider, four checkboxes (A–Z, a–z, 0–9, symbols) and crypto.getRandomValues. I assumed it was done. Then I went back to it while writing a blog post, and it had two problems. One was mostly theoretical. The other was very practical.

The original code 

let s = '';
if (up.checked) s += 'ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ';
if (lo.checked) s += 'abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz';
if (nu.checked) s += '0123456789';
if (sy.checked) s += '!@#$%^&*()-_=+[]{};:,.?';

const a = new Uint32Array(L);
crypto.getRandomValues(a);
let p = '';
for (let i = 0; i < L; i++) p += s[a[i] % s.length];

It uses a cryptographic RNG, so it looks fine. Here's what's wrong with it.

Problem 1: "Password must contain a number"

Ticking "0–9" only means digits are allowed. Nothing guarantees one shows up. With all four groups ticked, the combined set has 85 characters, and only 10 of them are digits.

I simulated 200,000 passwords at each length and counted how many were missing at least one of the ticked groups:

Length Missing a ticked group
6 70.6%
8 51.0%
12 26.5%
16 (my default) 14.6%

So roughly one in seven passwords at the default length would be rejected by a sign-up form that requires "at least one number and one symbol". The user ticked the boxes, copied the password, and the website said no. That's a real bug, not a theory.

Problem 2: modulo bias

a[i] % s.length maps 2³² possible values onto 85 characters. 2³² isn't a multiple of 85 (the remainder is 1), so one character gets picked very slightly more often than the others. Here the difference is about 2 in 10 billion, which nobody will ever exploit. But the fix is three lines, and it matters more when the set size is large relative to the random range. So:

// unbiased integer in [0, n)
function rnd(n) {
  const lim = Math.floor(2 ** 32 / n) * n;   // largest multiple of n
  const b = new Uint32Array(1);
  do { crypto.getRandomValues(b); } while (b[0] >= lim);
  return b[0] % n;
}

This is rejection sampling: throw away the few values from the incomplete top range and draw again. For small n a retry almost never happens.

The fix for problem 1

Pick one character from each ticked group first, fill the rest from the combined set, then shuffle so the guaranteed characters aren't always at the start:

const sets = [];   // only the ticked groups
// ...push each ticked group's characters...
const all = sets.join('');

const c = sets.map(g => g[rnd(g.length)]);   // one from each group
while (c.length < L) c.push(all[rnd(all.length)]);

for (let i = c.length - 1; i > 0; i--) {     // Fisher–Yates
  const j = rnd(i + 1);
  [c[i], c[j]] = [c[j], c[i]];
}
const password = c.join('');

I ran 20,000 passwords of length 6 with all groups ticked through the new version. All 20,000 contained every group.

Does guaranteeing one of each make the passwords weaker? Slightly, in theory, because the space is a little smaller than "any 16 of 85". In practice it's negligible. A 16-character password with all four groups is still around 100 bits of entropy, and the alternative is a password the website refuses.

The lesson

Using crypto.getRandomValues makes a generator secure. It doesn't make it correct. The bug that hurt users was in the logic around the RNG: what the checkboxes promise versus what the code guarantees. If you've written a generator like this, run a quick simulation over its output. It takes five minutes.

The generator is part of 14FreeTools, a set of free tools that run entirely in the browser. Nothing you generate is sent anywhere.

articles.title: I Built MLBox: A Browser Workbench That Shows How LLM Tokenizers Really Work
articles.description: Hi, I'm Mohit Verma, a Class 10 student from Patna, India, learning machine learning by building...
articles.body_html:
Hi, I'm Mohit Verma, a Class 10 student from Patna, India, learning machine learning by building things. MLBox is my open-source project: a browser workbench for LLM tokenizers, training intuition, and API pricing. Four tools, one static page, zero dependencies — every number is measured in your own browser.

Live demo: https://mohittt-vermaa.github.io/mlbox/
Code: https://github.com/mohittt-vermaa/mlbox

What's inside

Tokenizer lens — Paste any text and watch 7 real LLM tokenizers cut it up, token by token: counts, cost per million characters, a language cost matrix, a boundary diff between any two tokenizers, and a shareable link that freezes the whole comparison.

Micro playground — A neural net with hand-written backprop training live on canvas. Watch gradient descent solve XOR.

No-GPU recipes — 12 curated ML projects that genuinely finish on a laptop or a free Colab session, each with its one gotcha spelled out.

LLM price bench — 13 current models from 5 providers, transcribed from each provider's own pricing page with source links, plus a workload calculator and a real-prompt cost estimator.

The number that motivated all of this

Paste "नमस्ते दुनिया" ("hello world" in Hindi, 13 characters) and the tokenizers disagree: GPT-4o's tokenizer needs 5 tokens, Llama 3.1 needs 9, GPT-3.5/4's cl100k needs 13. Same two words, nearly 3x the bill depending on which tokenizer sits in front. Token choice is a cost multiplier and a context-window multiplier, and almost nobody looks at it.

Verified, not approximate

The tokenizer engine re-implements both BPE families in about 550 lines of dependency-free JavaScript, and the test suite checks it token-for-token against the upstream Rust implementations: 218,877 tokens, exact match on all seven models. There is also an Android app and a Windows desktop build in the releases, and everything runs offline with no API key and no backend — your text never leaves your machine.

Why I built it

I kept reading claims about token costs from blog posts instead of measuring them. MLBox is my way of learning ML properly: build the tool, verify every number, and share it so the next student can measure things themselves.

If it helps you, a star on GitHub means a lot: https://github.com/mohittt-vermaa/mlbox

— Mohit Verma
All my work: https://mohittt-vermaa.github.io

articles.title: I built a background remover that runs 100% in the browser. Here's how I made it 7x faster
articles.description: Most "free" background removers upload your photo to a server, run a model on a GPU, and then ask you...
articles.body_html:
Most "free" background removers upload your photo to a server, run a model on a GPU, and then ask you to pay for the full-resolution download. I wanted the opposite: the photo never leaves your device, the download is full resolution, and there is no account.

So I built Remove de Fundo, a background remover where the AI model runs entirely in the browser. The first version worked, but on real phones it was slow enough that people left before seeing a result. This post is about what made it slow and what fixed it.

End result on the same laptop and the same photo: 43.8 s → 6.4 s from click to cutout.

The stack

  • Astro for the site (static pages, deployed to Cloudflare Workers)
  • @imgly/background-removal with the IS-Net fp16 model (~88 MB)
  • ONNX Runtime Web, which runs the model with WebGPU on desktop and WebAssembly (CPU) on phones
  • A small post-processing step in canvas to clean up semi-transparent "haze" in the mask

Everything happens client-side. The server only serves static files.

Problem 1: the model came from a CDN that didn't cache

The first visit downloads ~100 MB (model + ONNX runtime). That is unavoidable for an in-browser model, but I noticed something worse: the CDN serving the model sent no Cache-Control header, and the edge marked it cf-cache-status: DYNAMIC. So returning visitors were often downloading the model again, and nothing was cached near the user.

Fix: self-host the model files. A build script downloads the model chunks once and puts them in public/ai/<version>/, and the library is pointed there with publicPath. Since the chunk file names are content hashes, they can be cached forever:

/ai/*
  Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable

Now a returning visitor loads the model from disk cache: zero network.

One gotcha: the chunk files have no extension, and both the dev server and the host treated extensionless paths as pages (404). Saving them as <hash>.bin and rewriting the names in resources.json fixed it.

Problem 2: the CPU path used one core out of eight

Phones always use the WebAssembly path, so CPU speed matters most. ONNX Runtime Web can use multiple threads, but only if the page is cross-origin isolated, because threads need SharedArrayBuffer.

My page wasn't isolated:

crossOriginIsolated // false

Fix: two headers.

Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin
Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: credentialless

I used credentialless instead of require-corp so Google Fonts and analytics keep working without CORP headers. Browsers that don't support it simply ignore it, so nothing breaks there.

Result (CPU, model already loaded): 22.7 s → 7.9 s per photo. Almost 3x, from two lines of config.

Problem 3: the bug that made PNG encoding 13x slower

After enabling isolation, inference got much faster but the total barely improved. I logged a timestamp for each stage and found this:

Stage Time
Inference 1.5 s
PNG encode 5.5 s
Edge refinement 4.4 s

Encoding a 1200 × 800 PNG should take a fraction of a second. I measured canvas.convertToBlob() on an idle page:

Page PNG encode
Not isolated 208 ms
Isolated, before loading ONNX 217 ms
Isolated, after running ONNX 2,648 ms

So isolation itself was fine. The problem: the library sets the WASM thread count to navigator.hardwareConcurrency (all cores), and ONNX's worker threads keep spin-waiting after inference. They occupy every core, and the browser's own image-encoding threads starve.

Fix: cap the thread count before the library loads. I used ONNX Runtime's own default (half the cores, at most 4) on CPU, and 1 thread on the GPU path, where the GPU does the work:

function limitOnnxThreads(device: 'gpu' | 'cpu') {
  const cores = navigator.hardwareConcurrency || 4;
  const threads = device === 'gpu' ? 1 : Math.max(1, Math.min(4, Math.ceil(cores / 2)));
  Object.defineProperty(navigator, 'hardwareConcurrency', {
    configurable: true,
    get: () => threads,
  });
}

Post-processing went from ~10 s back to 0.2 s.

Problem 4: the first photo on WebGPU paid for shader compilation

On the WebGPU path, the second photo took 2 s but the first took ~17 s on every page load. The session creation and, mostly, the first inference compile the GPU shaders.

Fix: warm up on intent. When the user hovers the upload area (desktop) or taps it (mobile), I:

  1. Prefetch the model files into the HTTP cache (low priority).
  2. Call the library's preload() with exactly the same config as the real run (the library memoizes the session by JSON.stringify(config)).
  3. On GPU only, run one throwaway inference on a tiny 32×32 image. The model input has a fixed size, so this compiles everything the real photo needs.

While the person is still picking a photo from their gallery, all of that is already happening. I skip the warm inference on CPU: on a phone it would take as long as a real cutout and the user's photo would wait behind it. I also skip prefetching on saveData or 2G connections, and on mobile only a tap on the upload box triggers it, so scrolling past doesn't burn 100 MB of someone's data.

Things I tried that didn't work

  • The smaller quantized model (isnet_quint8, 44 MB). Half the download, but it left patches of background all over a portrait. Not worth it.
  • Relying on HTTP heuristic caching for a third-party CDN. In practice, returning visitors still re-downloaded.

UX fixes that mattered as much as speed

  • The upload box was below the fold on a 730 px laptop screen. People saw a headline and left. Tightening the hero put the button in the first screen on laptops and phones.
  • Show the user's own photo with a scanning line while processing, instead of a generic spinner. It makes the wait feel much shorter.
  • On mobile, the label "Drag your photo here" makes no sense. It now says "Choose a photo".

Results

Before After
Click → result (laptop, first run) 43.8 s 6.4 s
CPU inference per photo 22.7 s 7.9 s
PNG encode + edge cleanup ~10 s (isolated, before fix) 0.2 s
Returning visitor model download often ~100 MB 0 (disk cache)

Since adding analytics, about 98% of removals succeed and more than half of the people who upload a photo download the result.

Credits

The heavy lifting is done by IMG.LY's background-removal-js (AGPL-3.0) and ONNX Runtime Web. If you build something similar, check their licenses.

You can try it here: removedefundo.com/en. It's free, with no sign-up, and works in English, Spanish and Portuguese. I'd love feedback, especially from people on older phones.

This post was written with AI assistance. The numbers come from real measurements on the live site.

articles.title: Long Exposure: a daguerreotype that takes a minute, because the SDK does
articles.description: This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge     In 1840 a portrait took a minute....
articles.body_html:
This is a submission for the Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge

In 1840 a portrait took a minute. You had to hold still. Your heart could not.

What I Built

Long Exposure is a portrait studio from 1840. You sit in front of your webcam for about a minute, keeping your head still and breathing normally, and a portrait develops on a silver plate. It is made only from what the SmartSpectra SDK reads through the camera which are the geometry of your face, your pulse, your breathing. No photograph of you is taken or kept.

The finished plate is alive. It flushes faintly in time with your real pulse, and the bust rises and falls with your own recorded breaths. Turn it over, and the back (the verso) shows the evidence: the raw readouts, how the beats were timed, your pulse waveform when the signal was strong enough to draw, and a timestamped log of the sitting.

Why a minute? The SDK needs time before each signal is reliable: about 12 seconds for the pulse, about 30 for the breathing. Most apps hide that wait behind a spinner. Long Exposure makes the wait the point. 1840 cameras needed a long exposure too, and sitters had to keep still for it. Here the exposure stages follow the SDK's own warm-up:

Exposure Stage What the SDK provides What you see
0–12 s Focusing 478 face landmarks A ghost of your face emerges as engraving on silver
12–30 s The heart Pulse waveform and rate A flush travels from forehead to chin on each beat, with a soft heartbeat sound
30–60 s The breath Breathing rate and chest trace The bust rises and falls with your chest, and goes still when you hold your breath
60 s+ Fixing A locked pulse A guilloché seal drawn from this sitting rhythm is engraved in the corner

A stage only starts when the SDK says it signal is ready: marked stable, or for the pulse, a confidence of at least 40. The plate never pretends. If a signal never settles, the plate develops underexposed and says which signal was missing.

The studio is strict, the way a 19th-century photographer was:

  • Talking caps the lens (after a second and a half, so a stray word does not). The exposure clock stops, and the cap is logged.
  • Moving, poor light, or leaving the frame caps it too, and the caption says what to fix.
  • A second face caps it at once. If it stays for two seconds, the sitting ends and everything is discarded. The plate is for one consenting sitter.

Under the plate, a kymograph scratches your live pulse and chest trace as they arrive, like the soot-drum recorders of the 1800s. The front never shows a number.

Double Exposure: load a friend's saved plate and the two portraits sit side by side, each beating in its own rhythm.

Demo

Try it in your browser, no install or key: long-exposure-brown.vercel.app. Press Watch a real sitting to play back a real sitting recorded with the SDK. A live sitting needs the desktop app and your own SmartSpectra key (instructions in the repo).

The video is one live take. Only the camera warm-up and the wait for my breath are sped up, the heart and breath stages play in real time. The video has no sound because my screen recorder didn't capture the app's audio. In the app, each flush comes with a soft heartbeat sound. At about 0:48 someone walked behind me: the plate darkens with "Someone else is in frame", then recovers when they leave. I kept it in.

Code

TimothyBabatu13 / long-exposure

Long Exposure

A finished plate from a real recorded sitting: it brightens on each heartbeat and breathes with the sitter's recorded breaths.

A 60-second living daguerreotype. You sit for a portrait, as people did in 1840. The plate develops while you keep your head still and breathe normally, and the finished portrait flushes at the pace of your real pulse and breathes with your own recorded breaths. No photograph of you is taken or kept.

Try it in your browser, no install or key: long-exposure-brown.vercel.app. Press Watch a real sitting to play back a real 90-second sitting recorded with the SDK.

Built for the DEV Presage SmartSpectra SDK Challenge with @smartspectra/node-sdk.

In 1840 a portrait took a minute. You had to hold still. Your heart couldn't.

How a sitting works

The SDK needs time before each signal is reliable: about 12 s for pulse and 30 s for…

View on GitHub

How It Responds to Human Signals

Every live signal has one job on the plate, and nothing on the plate moves without one:

SDK signal What it does, in real time
Face landmarks (478 points) Draw the portrait itself, and the framing guide
Pulse rate and waveform Start the heart stage, and time the flush and the heartbeat sound
Breathing rate and chest trace Start the breath stage, and make the bust rise and fall
Talking Caps the lens, the way a photographer would stop you talking
Smile A smile held for three seconds is engraved into the plate
HRV, when the SDK marks it stable Can settle the rhythm for the seal
Validation status (face, light, movement) Caps the lens and tells you what to fix

The kymograph under the plate draws the pulse and chest traces as the packets arrive, so you can watch the plate respond.

How I built it

  • Electron + TypeScript. The SDK runs natively in the main process. My first version used the SDK's renderer path, which copies every camera frame from the window to the main process. On my 4-core laptop that delivered only 8–18 of the camera's 30 frames per second, and the SDK stopped with kSustainedLowFrameRate. Reading the camera natively keeps the frames inside the SDK, so the window only receives the decoded results: a few kilobytes.
  • The portrait is drawn, not photographed. One WebGL fragment shader turns face geometry into a lit, engraved silver plate in a stamped brass mat. No camera pixel is ever drawn into the portrait.
  • Beats, honestly. The flush lands on beats detected in the SDK's pulse waveform when it arrives early enough. Otherwise it falls back to beats predicted from recent intervals, or to the SDK's pulse rate. The verso says which method was used. In the sitting in the video the waveform was too faint, so the beats were spaced from the SDK's averaged pulse rate, and the verso says exactly that rather than claiming more.
  • Stability first. The breath stage waits for the SDK's stable flag. The heart stage waits for stable or a pulse confidence of at least 40, plus a beat timing the tracker can trust. The flag flickers from packet to packet, so a signal counts as ready if it was ready within the last 15 seconds.
  • Tests. 56 unit tests cover the sitting state machine, beat and breath tracking, the loop, and the plate file. CI runs typecheck and tests on every push. Recorded sittings replay through the same pipeline.

A tip for other SmartSpectra builders. If your Electron app stops with error 14 (low frame rate), move the SDK to the main process with useCamera(), and send the decoded metrics to the window.

Credits. GIF export uses gifenc by Matt DesLauriers (MIT). Everything else is my own code on top of the SmartSpectra Node SDK.

Lineage. Rafael Lozano-Hemmer's Pulse Room made heartbeats into public light. Long Exposure makes one heartbeat into a private portrait, and gives it back to the sitter.

Prize Categories

Most Creative or Delightful Use.

What inspired it. The SDK's first minute. Pulse takes about 12 seconds to settle and breathing about 30, and the usual answer to that is a loading spinner. Then I remembered that early daguerreotypes also took about a minute, and sitters had to hold still the whole time, sometimes with an iron head brace. The wait was the same length, so I made the wait the experience.

What makes it original. Vital signs are usually shown as numbers and charts. Here they are a portrait instead: your pulse is a warm flush on silver, your breath is the bust rising and falling, and the plate back is the only place a number appears. The SDK's limits become the studio's rules: talking caps the lens because the SDK can't read you while you talk, and a second face ends the sitting because the plate is for one person.

What's playful or unexpected. You get a portrait with no photograph in it, one that keeps breathing after you've left the chair. You can load a friend's saved plate beside yours, and the two beat out of step, each in its own rhythm.

Consent and Data Handling

Written with Presage's Telemetry and Privacy notes in hand.

  • Nothing happens until you agree. The camera opens only after you read the sitting agreement and press I agree to sit. There is no auto-start and no background mode.
  • One consenting person. A second face caps the lens at once, and ends the sitting (discarding everything) if it stays for two seconds. Each sitter agrees for themselves; the privacy notes ask a parent or guardian to sit with a minor and agree for them.
  • No photographs. Camera frames stay inside the SDK. Long Exposure never stores or exports them, and the portrait is never drawn from them. One exception, off by default: the Show me the camera option opens a live mirror beside the plate so you can check your framing. It is shown only, never recorded or saved.
  • Memory only. Decoded signals and the finished plate live in memory until you press Sit again or Leave the studio (one click, always visible, wipes everything).
  • Exports only where you choose. The GIF, PNGs and .plate.json go through a save dialog. A plate holds no photograph, but it is derived from your body (face geometry, heart and breath rhythm), and the app says so. Share it as you would a photo.
  • What leaves the device. The app's page makes no network requests: it runs under a strict Content Security Policy, and the main process blocks and logs any request. The SDK contacts Presage to check the API key and meter usage. Presage telemetry is off by default.
  • Deliberately not used: the stress index, emotion scores, and the SDK's AI insights. The only expression read is the smile, a smile held for three seconds is engraved into the plate. The app makes no judgement about how you feel or how healthy you are.

Network audit (Windows 11, telemetry off, live session of about five minutes; every TCP connection owned by the app, sampled twice a second):

Time Process Host What it is
23–30 s main (SDK) cont-api.physiology.presagetech.com:443 SDK start-up: key check and model download
252 s main (SDK) cont-api.physiology.presagetech.com:443 The SDK's periodic usage check

No other host was contacted. Full method and limits: PRIVACY.md.

Not a medical device. Long Exposure is portraiture. It does not diagnose, monitor or treat anything. The numbers on the verso are there only as evidence that the portrait responded to a real, live signal.

What I'd do next

  • More sitters, skin tones and lighting. My live sittings are all one person, in one room.
  • Exact beat timing (waveform tier) on faster machines.
  • Blinks that reliably leave ghost eyes. The SDK's blink flag was too sparse in my sittings, and the face landmarks were too coarse to detect blinks myself.

If you sit for a plate, post its GIF in the comments. I'd love to see your heart.

articles.title: The Week My App Almost Ran Out of Database
articles.description: Hey dev.to — Lepp again. Entry two in building Neuro-Kindred (a free, calm social app for...
articles.body_html:
Hey dev.to — Lepp again. Entry two in building Neuro-Kindred (a free, calm social app for neurodivergent adults, 18+) in the open. Last time: pebbles instead of likes. This time: a mystery, three wrong suspects, and the week I nearly lost the whole app to a free-tier limit.

The setup

Neuro-Kindred runs on a $3/month server and a free Postgres database (Neon, 100 free compute-hours a month). On Nov 15 I got the email nobody wants: 80 of the 100 hours already used, halfway through the month. At 100, the database sleeps until December 1st — app down, no charge, data safe, but down.

Something was waking the database constantly. It wasn't my members: in the worst 48-hour stretch, 38 members sent 63 messages total. So I went hunting.

Suspect #1: the scanners

The server logs showed a burst of 188 requests in one minute from a cloud IP, probing for .env files and admin paths. All 404s, nothing exposed — but bots were my first theory. Verdict: real, but too small. The burn continued on quiet nights with no scanner traffic at all.

Suspect #2: the old deployment

The app used to live on an app-builder platform before I moved it to my own server. Maybe the old copy was still running somewhere, pinging away? I unpublished it (Nov 17) and measured for 24 hours. The burn barely moved. Not the culprit — and now I couldn't easily un-unpublish my main suspect.

Suspect #3: my own forgotten robots

This one stung. Back in September, the builder era set up two keep-alive jobs (duplicates, of course) pinging the app's health endpoint every 5 minutes — and every ping runs database queries, and every query resets the database's 5-minute idle timer. The database was being politely woken up 24/7 by robots I owned. I disabled both (Nov 15) and the sleep test passed... but the daily burn only dropped a little. A contributor. Not the culprit.

The actual culprit: the app itself

The final measurement read the request logs by endpoint. In 48 hours: the calls screen had been checked 3,497 times — about once every 3 seconds — from one or two phones with the page left open. Message threads every 4–5 seconds. Game rooms every 2 seconds. My own app's screens were the waker. One member leaving the app open on their phone was costing more database than every real conversation combined.

The fix shipped Nov 20: the calls overview now checks every 20 seconds, message threads every 10 (pausing entirely when the tab is hidden was already in there — the problem was never hidden tabs, it was visible ones being impatient). Full test suite green (552 tests), and I'm re-measuring for 24 hours before I claim it worked. If the number doesn't drop, I'll say so in entry three.

The honest numbers

  • Database: 86.3 of 100 free hours used (Nov 18 reading)
  • Members: 38 · Revenue: $0 · Server: $3/month
  • Cost of the investigation: a few evenings and one unpublished old site

Lesson: on a free tier, your own polling is your biggest user. Measure by endpoint before you blame the internet.

One question before you go

Neuro-Kindred runs a community night every Friday, 7pm CT (trivia, a game, then a watch-together on Discord) — it's the hour the app feels most like itself. Comment with the interest you could talk about for a full hour, and I'll send you an invite to this Friday's. That's the whole exchange — your weird topic for a seat at the table. It's also literally what the app is for.

— Lepp

Next entry: "Pebbles grow old now" — why an unanswered pebble sitting in limbo forever is unkind, and the 30-day close we just shipped.

articles.title: The Most Dangerous AI-Generated Test Is the One That Passes
articles.description: AI can generate a browser test in seconds.  You give it a URL and ask it to verify that the search...
articles.body_html:
AI can generate a browser test in seconds.

You give it a URL and ask it to verify that the search feature works. It opens the page, enters a search term, checks that some results appear, and produces a test.

You execute it. Green.

You run it ten more times. Still green.

Then a customer reports that the search results disappear when they press the browser's Back button.

Your automated test never caught it.

The problem wasn't that the AI generated invalid code. The code worked exactly as written.

The problem was that nobody questioned what the test was actually proving.

And I think this is one of the biggest risks with the current wave of AI-powered test automation.

A passing test doesn't necessarily mean a working feature

Let's take a typical e-commerce application.

The search page has a few common behaviors:

  • Results update after the user stops typing.
  • The search query is reflected in the URL.
  • Refreshing the page preserves the search.
  • Opening a product and pressing Back restores the previous results.
  • Slow API responses don't cause stale results to appear.

A human tester familiar with the application might consider all five behaviors important.

But ask an AI agent to "test the product search," and it might generate something like this:

import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('product search works', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/products');

  await page.getByPlaceholder('Search products')
    .fill('wireless');

  await expect(
    page.getByText('Wireless Headset')
  ).toBeVisible();
});

Is this a valid test?

Sure.

Does it prove that product search works?

Only in a very narrow sense.

It doesn't verify the URL, navigation history, request ordering, or what happens when the page is refreshed.

And because the test passes, the team might never notice those missing scenarios.

The missing assertions are more dangerous than flaky assertions

Flaky tests get attention because they interrupt CI pipelines.

Missing assertions are quieter.

They don't fail. They don't generate alerts. They don't slow down deployments.

They simply leave important behavior untested.

Consider a search field that uses debouncing.

If a user types "wireless headset," the application might wait 300 milliseconds after the last keystroke before sending the search request.

This reduces unnecessary API calls.

But now imagine two requests arrive out of order.

The user searches for "wireless," then quickly changes the term to "wireless headset."

The newer request completes first. The correct results appear.

A moment later, the older request completes and replaces them with results for "wireless."

The UI is now showing stale data.

A basic test might miss this entirely.

Similarly, the application might display the correct results but fail to synchronize the URL, making its search state impossible to preserve through navigation.

The guide Testing Debounced Search, URL Sync, and Back-Button State Without Flaky Assertions covers these kinds of scenarios and explains why outcome-based assertions are generally more reliable than hard-coded delays.

Here's a more useful browser test for an application where search state is stored in the URL:

import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('search survives navigation and refresh', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('/products');

  const search = page.getByRole('searchbox', {
    name: /search/i
  });

  await search.fill('wireless');

  // Verify that search state reaches the URL.
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/products\?q=wireless$/);

  // Verify a meaningful search result.
  const product = page.getByRole('link', {
    name: 'Wireless Headset'
  });

  await expect(product).toBeVisible();

  // Navigate to the product and return.
  await product.click();
  await page.goBack();

  // The previous search should be restored.
  await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/products\?q=wireless$/);
  await expect(search).toHaveValue('wireless');
  await expect(product).toBeVisible();

  // Refresh should preserve the same state.
  await page.reload();

  await expect(search).toHaveValue('wireless');
  await expect(product).toBeVisible();
});

This example assumes the application provides these accessibility labels and URL conventions.

Notice what's missing from the test: waitForTimeout(300).

We're testing the behavior, not the implementation detail of how long the debounce timer takes.

That makes the test both more useful and less sensitive to timing differences.

It still doesn't cover out-of-order API responses. That deserves a separate test with controlled response ordering.

The point is that a good suite covers distinct risks, rather than generating multiple variations of the same happy path.

What if the UI is correct but the API contract has changed?

Here's another problem that AI-generated browser tests can miss.

Suppose the search API used to return:

{
  "id": 123,
  "name": "Wireless Headset",
  "price": 79.99
}

After a backend update, it starts returning:

{
  "id": 123,
  "name": "Wireless Headset",
  "price": "79.99"
}

The price field changed from a number to a string.

The browser might still render $79.99 correctly.

Your end-to-end test passes.

But another consumer of that API might fail because it expects a numeric value.

This is schema drift, and it's one reason browser tests shouldn't be your only line of defense.

A useful API testing strategy should verify response contracts, not just HTTP status codes.

It should also help teams reproduce failures using mocks or stubs, and preserve enough information to explain why a CI run failed.

There's a practical selection rubric in Schema Drift, Mock Support, and CI Failure Evidence: What to Look for in API Testing Tools.

You don't need to perform every assertion through a browser.

In fact, trying to force all testing into the end-to-end layer usually makes your suite slower and more expensive to maintain.

The browser should verify what the user experiences. API and contract tests should verify the assumptions that different services make about each other.

AI should generate drafts, not unquestionable truth

This brings us back to AI.

The promise is attractive: generate automated tests from natural-language instructions, reduce scripting work, and create broader coverage faster.

There's real value in that.

But the part that deserves more attention is what happens after the test is generated.

Can someone read the steps?

Can they modify an assertion?

Can they understand why the AI chose a particular action?

Can they reject a generated test before it becomes part of the release pipeline?

And if the AI modifies an existing test to accommodate a UI change, can someone review that modification?

Imagine an automated test failing because the Checkout button disappeared.

An AI self-healing mechanism might find another button and successfully click it.

That's useful if the button was simply renamed.

It's dangerous if the AI silently selected a different action.

A previously failing test can become green without the underlying problem being fixed.

The article Human Review Is the Feature: Choosing AI Testing Tools That Keep You in Control examines exactly these considerations, including editable steps, approval workflows, rollback capabilities, and the evidence available to reviewers.

For most teams, I think the sensible approach is straightforward.

Use AI to accelerate test creation and maintenance.

But keep the expected behavior, critical assertions, and acceptance criteria under human control.

The goal should be to reduce repetitive work, not remove accountability.

More tests also means more test management

There's a less exciting consequence of AI-generated automation.

Once generating tests becomes cheap, teams can end up with thousands of them.

Some are duplicates.

Some validate trivial behavior.

Some are based on outdated requirements.

Others were generated for features that no longer exist.

And someone eventually has to figure out which tests matter.

This is where test management becomes important.

Not because every automated test needs a lengthy approval process, but because a team needs some way to connect test cases with requirements, ownership, execution results, and releases.

Tools such as Qase and TestRail approach that problem differently.

The comparison Qase vs TestRail: Less Process Overhead Without Losing Test Visibility examines the tradeoff between a lighter workflow and more structured test management.

That distinction becomes increasingly relevant when AI generates tests faster than people can review them.

A small team might need a lightweight system that makes it easy to organize cases and eliminate duplication.

A larger organization might need stricter controls around ownership, revisions, and release reporting.

Either way, generating additional tests isn't automatically equivalent to improving coverage.

A suite with 500 carefully maintained tests can be more valuable than a suite with 5,000 tests nobody fully understands.

In regulated environments, green isn't enough

The stakes change when automated tests are used in healthcare, financial services, insurance, or other regulated environments.

Imagine an AI agent modifies a test covering a payment approval workflow.

The updated test passes.

Six months later, an auditor asks:

Who modified the test?

Why was it changed?

Who approved the modification?

Which version executed before the release?

What evidence was preserved?

A screenshot showing a green checkmark won't answer those questions.

Organizations with formal audit requirements need traceability across test creation, modification, approval, execution, and evidence retention.

That's why choosing an AI testing platform for a regulated environment involves more than comparing how effectively the tools generate tests.

The guide Regulated Teams Need Different AI Testing Platforms looks at audit logs, approval workflows, role-based permissions, evidence export, and retention policies.

Not every product needs those controls.

A small SaaS startup can usually operate with much less ceremony.

But for regulated teams, the ability to reconstruct what happened during a release may be just as important as the test result itself.

And introducing AI into the workflow doesn't eliminate those requirements.

It makes clearly defined responsibilities even more important.

A simple rule for reviewing AI-generated tests

Before accepting an AI-generated test into a production test suite, I'd ask the reviewer to answer four questions.

1. What user behavior does this test actually prove?

Not what the test is called. Not what the prompt asked the AI to generate. What does the execution really verify?

2. Could the feature be broken while this test still passes?

Think about stale data, missing persistence, wrong API responses, navigation behavior, and alternative paths.

This question alone often reveals missing assertions.

3. If the test fails, will someone understand why?

A useful test should produce enough context to investigate the problem without spending an hour reproducing it manually.

4. Can we safely review and reverse changes to the test?

This matters especially when AI tools can modify existing tests or update locators automatically.

If the generated test cannot pass these four questions, it probably isn't ready to become part of your regression suite.

The real opportunity with AI in testing

I don't think AI-generated test automation is a bad idea.

Quite the opposite.

Creating automated tests has traditionally required too much repetitive work, especially when translating human-readable test cases into scripts.

AI can help reduce that effort substantially.

But I wouldn't measure success by the number of tests an AI agent generates.

I'd look at how many meaningful failures those tests catch, how much time they save during maintenance, and how quickly engineers can investigate failures.

Most importantly, I'd look at whether the team understands what its tests are actually validating.

Because there's a big difference between automating a browser interaction and proving that a feature works.

AI is making the first one much easier.

The second one still requires engineering judgment.

And that's probably a good thing.

articles.title: Your Sticky Header Is Hiding Anchor Links. `scroll-margin-top` Fixes It.
articles.description: Clicking a table-of-contents link lands the heading right behind your sticky nav, half-hidden. The fix isn't a JavaScript scroll offset — it's one CSS property the browser already checks before it scrolls.
articles.body_html:
You redesign a docs page. Sticky header, clean table of contents down the side, the kind of polish that makes a demo look finished. Then someone clicks "Installation" in the TOC, and the page jumps — except the "Installation" heading is now sitting behind the header, top third clipped off, like the scroll stopped one beat too early.

It's not a bug in your heading. It's not a bug in the TOC link. The browser scrolled exactly where you told it to. You just never told it about the header.

The obvious fix that didn't quite work

The TOC links are plain anchors: <a href="#installation">. The browser handles the jump on its own — no JavaScript required, which is exactly why it feels like it shouldn't need any. So the first fix is the one that feels native to the problem: intercept the click, do the math yourself.

document.querySelectorAll('a[href^="#"]').forEach((link) => {
  link.addEventListener("click", (e) => {
    e.preventDefault();
    const id = link.getAttribute("href").slice(1);
    const target = document.getElementById(id);
    const headerHeight = document.querySelector("header").offsetHeight;
    window.scrollTo({
      top: target.getBoundingClientRect().top + window.scrollY - headerHeight - 16,
      behavior: "smooth",
    });
  });
});

It works. Click a TOC link, the heading lands below the header, clean. Ship it, close the ticket.

Then QA files three more:

  • Deep-linking straight to yoursite.com/docs#installation — no click ever fired — still lands the heading behind the header, because the hack only runs on click.
  • The browser's native back/forward button restores the old scroll position, not yours — hitting Back after a TOC click snaps right back behind the header.
  • Mobile ships a taller header. headerHeight was read once on load; resize the window and the offset is stale until a reload.

Each of those is a separate bug with a separate fix — handle DOMContentLoaded for the deep-link case, listen for popstate, re-read offsetHeight on resize. You're not patching one bug anymore. You're reimplementing the browser's own "scroll to this element" logic, one missed case at a time, in a <script> tag.

The browser already asks "how much space do you need"

Fragment navigation, Element.scrollIntoView(), and the browser scrolling a focused element into view as you tab through the page all go through the same question: what counts as "this element is now in view"? Since 2021, every major browser has agreed on an answer CSS checks before any of them run — scroll-margin-top and its counterpart, scroll-padding-top.

Put it on the headings themselves:

h2,
h3 {
  scroll-margin-top: 4.5rem; /* roughly the header's height, plus breathing room */
}

That's it. No click handler, no preventDefault(), no recomputed pixel offset. Click a TOC link, hit the browser's native back button, paste a #installation link straight into the address bar — every path the browser uses to bring that heading into view now stops 4.5rem early, because the browser itself is doing the arithmetic, the same way it always has.

Per-heading vs. whole-page: pick the one that matches the bug

scroll-margin-top goes on the target — the thing being scrolled to. scroll-padding-top goes on the scroll container — usually html, or whatever element actually scrolls — and applies the same offset to every target inside it, without touching each heading individually:

html {
  scroll-padding-top: 4.5rem; /* one declaration, covers every #anchor on the site */
}

If every page on the site sits under the same sticky header, scroll-padding-top on html is the one-line, whole-site fix — set it once, forget it. Reach for scroll-margin-top on specific elements instead when different targets need different offsets: a shorter mobile header, a taller "in-page alert" banner above certain sections, or a card in a horizontally-scrolling carousel that needs its own left-edge margin rather than a top one.

🎮 Try it yourself

▶️ Open the interactive playground →

Runs right in your browser — poke at it and watch the concept react live.

Stop hardcoding the header's height as a magic number

4.5rem is a guess that goes stale the day someone adds a banner to the header. Read the header's real height instead, and feed it in as a custom property:

:root {
  --header-h: 64px; /* kept in sync with the header's actual rendered height */
}

h2,
h3 {
  scroll-margin-top: calc(var(--header-h) + 16px);
}

const header = document.querySelector("header");
const setHeaderHeight = () =>
  document.documentElement.style.setProperty("--header-h", `${header.offsetHeight}px`);

setHeaderHeight();
new ResizeObserver(setHeaderHeight).observe(header);

Now the only JavaScript left is measuring the header — not re-deriving the browser's entire scroll-to-element behavior. If the header grows a second row on mobile, ResizeObserver catches it and the custom property updates; scroll-margin-top reads the new value on the next scroll. The division of labor is the point: JavaScript's job shrinks to "report one number," and CSS's job — "stop scrolling here" — stays where the browser already does it for free.

Where this still needs a human

scroll-margin-top fixes where the page lands. It doesn't fix a heading that's visually ambiguous about whether it's "the current section" once it's sitting right under the header edge — that's a design question about header contrast and spacing, not a CSS-property question. And if your TOC also needs to highlight the active section as the reader scrolls, that's a separate job (usually IntersectionObserver), not something scroll-margin-top does for you. It solves exactly one problem — stopping short of the header — and it's worth not asking it to solve the other two.

🧠 Test yourself

Think it clicked? Take the 7-question quiz →

Instant feedback, a hint on every question, and an explanation for each answer — right or wrong.

The bug report wasn't "the table of contents is broken." It was "the browser doesn't know about your header" — and it turns out the browser was willing to be told, in CSS, for free, since before most of us noticed. Got a scroll offset hack sitting in a click handler somewhere? Go check what it's actually compensating for — there's a decent chance one property replaces it.

articles.title: A Bitcoin Cash covenant that pays your network fee, and why you pay it back in dollars
articles.description: Someone pays you $20 in PUSD, a dollar token on Bitcoin Cash. You try to send $5 of it on, and your...
articles.body_html:
Someone pays you $20 in PUSD, a dollar token on Bitcoin Cash. You try to send $5 of it on, and your wallet may refuse: every transaction needs a miner fee paid in BCH, and you hold none you can spend. The usual answer is "go buy some BCH first", which is exactly where a new user stops.

I built FeePass for BCH BLAZE 2026 to remove that step. It is live on mainnet, the code is on GitHub, and the first sponsored send is on chain: d59f120b…f8b7. This post is about the one design decision that shaped everything else: why the sender still pays, and why they pay in dollars.

The shape: one ordinary transaction

A FeePass send is a single transaction with a fixed shape:

  • in0 is your PUSD coin, signed by your own wallet.
  • in1 is one "lane" of a sponsor pool: a UTXO locked by a CashScript covenant. Nobody signs it.
  • out0 sends PUSD to the recipient, out1 is your PUSD change.
  • out2 is the lane going back to the pool, minus the miner fee, plus exactly 0.01 PUSD.

The lane's BCH pays the miner. Your wallet never touches BCH. On mainnet that first send looked like this: 572 bytes, a 580-sat miner fee paid by the lane, and the sender's spendable BCH was 0 before and 0 after.

The wall: a covenant cannot remember you

My first idea was the obvious one: free sends, a few per person. A paymaster with a budget.

That does not survive contact with a covenant. A covenant is a spending condition on one coin. It can read the transaction it is being spent in (inputs, outputs, values, token amounts) through native introspection, but it has no memory across transactions and no notion of "a person". A rule like "at most 3 free sends per user" needs to know who the user is and what they did yesterday. Any limit keyed to an address is defeated by generating a fresh address, which costs nothing. Free sends from a covenant are drainable by anyone with a loop.

You can move that memory off-chain into a server that co-signs every transaction, which is roughly how fee-payer relayers work elsewhere. But then the sponsor key is online, the server is the trust model, and the rule no longer lives on chain.

The fix: make every send pay for itself

So the covenant does not try to recognise anyone. Instead, every send must leave the pool better off in dollars than it was in sats:

// R4 hard per-transaction cap on what the lane can lose.
require(tx.outputs[2].value >= tx.inputs[1].value - maxSubsidy);

// R5 the pool receives exactly feeTokens PUSD: never less, never more.
require(tx.outputs[2].tokenCategory == pusdCategory);
require(tx.outputs[2].tokenAmount == tx.inputs[1].tokenAmount + feeTokens);

maxSubsidy is 2,000 sats: the most one lane can lose in one transaction. feeTokens is 1 base unit of PUSD, which is 0.01 PUSD. As long as 0.01 PUSD is worth more than 2,000 sats, draining the pool costs the attacker more than it takes, no matter how many addresses they generate. The deploy script refuses parameters without a 1.5× margin; at the price it checked when the lane was funded (BCH $192.64), a standard send costs the lane 580 sats, about $0.0011, and pays the pool $0.01.

It is an equality on purpose. "At least 0.01 PUSD" would let a buggy client overpay; "exactly" means the pool's side of the transaction is fully determined.

The rest of the rules

The covenant's paid path is short enough to read in one sitting. The full file is contracts/FeePassPool.cash:

function sponsorPaid() {
    // R1 fixed shape: exactly one user input, one pool input, three outputs.
    require(tx.inputs.length == 2);
    require(tx.outputs.length == 3);
    require(this.activeInputIndex == 1);

    // R2 the user brings PUSD and sends PUSD.
    require(tx.inputs[0].tokenCategory == pusdCategory);
    require(tx.outputs[0].tokenCategory == pusdCategory);

    // R3 the lane returns to the same covenant.
    require(tx.outputs[2].lockingBytecode == tx.inputs[1].lockingBytecode);

    // R6 the user-side outputs may exceed the user's input sats by at most maxTopUp
    require(tx.outputs[0].value + tx.outputs[1].value <= tx.inputs[0].value + maxTopUp);
    // ... R4, R5, R7, R8
}

R6 exists because token outputs need dust. A partial PUSD send creates two token outputs of about 650 sats each, and a small user coin may not carry enough. The lane may top that up by at most 675 sats per send. On the first mainnet send, the lane's total cost was 882 sats: the 580-sat miner fee plus 302 sats of dust top-up.

What the covenant deliberately does not check

It does not pick the recipient. The pool only enforces its own side: shape, cap, and the fee coming back. Who gets paid is bound by the sender's own signature, SIGHASH_ALL|FORKID|UTXOS (0x61), over input 0. The app asks the wallet to sign only that input over WizardConnect, then verifies the signed transaction on the BCH VM before broadcasting it.

Two senders, one lane

A lane's change can be spent again before it confirms, so two people can grab the same lane at once. The second broadcast fails with txn-mempool-conflict. The app then picks another random open lane and asks the wallet for one more signature with the same coin, at most twice. Reusing the same coin matters: only one version of your payment can ever confirm.

Honest limits

  • One lane is funded today; 20 is the target. Concurrency is real but thin.
  • The first mainnet send was signed by a headless test key through the app's own builder and VM check, not by a named wallet. Whether a given wallet accepts a request to sign one input with sighash 0x61 is exactly what the in-app wallet gate records; none is verified yet.
  • "No spendable BCH" is not "zero BCH": a token coin always carries a few hundred sats of dust.
  • The fee is fixed at deploy, not oracle-priced. The covenant bounds each send, not the pool's total.

Try it

Open feepass.edycu.dev, connect a WizardConnect wallet, claim 0.25 starter PUSD if you have none, and send 0.10 PUSD. The ticket shows your spendable BCH before and after, read from the chain. Judges and the curious can start at the 60-second page.

Code, tests (189 unit and covenant VM tests, 32 end-to-end) and every mainnet txid: github.com/edycutjong/feepass.

articles.title: My search box scored 1.00 on a query it understood nothing about
articles.description: A visitor typed "18 m high, 8 m wide". The fallback returned a rebar hook table and a brick chart, both at 1.00 confidence. Both matched because their index text contains the string "180".
articles.body_html:
On 21 November someone typed 18米高8米宽 into the search box on my site. That means "18 m high, 8 m wide" — a question about scaffolding, arriving from a comment thread about a job site. The search returned a table of rebar hook lengths and a chart of bricks per cubic metre of masonry.

Both results were served at a relevance score of 1.00.

The query contains no noun. Not one. It is two dimensions and nothing else, and my matcher looked at it and said: perfect match, here you go.

This is about the arithmetic that made that inevitable, why the obvious fixes don't help, and the four-line gate that replaced a scoring problem with a refusal to guess.

The failure has two stages, and the first one behaved correctly

Search on the site is a plain substring AND over an index string per card. Each card carries a data-k attribute — title, category, a one-line description, the slug, and a handful of pinyin and synonym aliases. Stage one requires every whitespace-separated token of the query to appear somewhere in that string.

// stage 1
n = apply(function (key) {
  for (var i = 0; i < toks.length; i++) {
    if (key.indexOf(toks[i]) < 0) return false;
  }
  return true;
});

Chinese has no spaces, so 18米高8米宽 is one token, and no index string contains it. Zero results. That is correct for stage one, and it is why stage two exists: people type questions, the index stores nouns, and substring matching won't bridge that on its own.

Stage two is a 2-gram fallback. Split the query into CJK bigrams and alphanumeric runs, drop segments that appear nowhere in the index, then score every card:

var gs = raw.match(/[a-z0-9]+|[\u4e00-\u9fff]+/g);   // segment the query
// CJK segment → all overlapping 2-grams; ASCII/digits → kept whole
score = hits / valid.length;                          // fraction of grams found
if (max >= 0.5) showEverythingTiedAtMax();

That "drop segments that appear nowhere" step is the clever part, and it is normally what makes this kind of fallback work at all. A user types 一米多重怎么算; 怎么算 exists on no card, so counting it in the denominator would cap every real match at 20%. Filtering noise out of the denominator is what lets the signal win.

On this query, the filter did its job perfectly — and that is the problem. 米高 and 米宽 are not in the index. Neither is anything else. What survived was the digits.

The score is hits / tokens, which rewards queries it understands least

Two grams survived, so the denominator was 2, so one hit scored 0.5 and cleared the threshold. Required matches is always ceil(n/2): four grams need two, two grams need one, and a single-gram query needs a hit to score a flat 1.00.

Read that back: the less of the query the parser could keep, the lower the bar to answer it. Confidence and comprehension move in opposite directions — the exact inversion of what a relevance score should mean.

The index has 238 cards and 4,204 distinct CJK bigrams, and the frequency distribution is brutally top-heavy:

Bigram Cards containing it Share of index
算器 206 86.6%
计算 187 78.6%
用量 64 26.9%
面积 61 25.6%

Every card title ends in "calculator", so any fragment of that word is universal. A two-gram query where one gram is 计算 scores 0.5 everywhere before it has found out what the page is about.

What the two grams actually were

Here is the part I did not expect. The surviving grams were 18 and 8, and two cards contain both. Both contain them because both index strings contain the number 180:

  • the rebar hook page, whose index text includes 180度弯钩 — a 180-degree hook;
  • the brick table, whose index text includes 120 / 180 / 240 — wall thicknesses in millimetres.

18 and 8 are substrings of 180. One page means degrees, the other means millimetres, and the scoring function saw identical evidence in both. The 1.00 was not a measurement of relevance. It was a coincidence of string layout, and it happened to land on exactly the two cards whose numbers differ in unit from the question that was asked.

Digit fragments are rare in the index, which made the coincidence look like a signal:

Fragment Cards containing it Share
18 2 1%
8 5 2%
1 13 5%
5 14 6%

And because the fallback shows everything tied at the maximum in build order rather than by score, the answer was stable, reproducible, and arbitrary. 1.5米 produced seven cards at 1.00 for the same reason: grams 1 and 5, one hit each, seven winners.

Rarity doesn't rescue you

The reflex fix is IDF — weight rare grams up, common grams down. It makes this worse. 18 appears on 2 of 238 cards, so it is maximally rare, so IDF would push its weight to the ceiling and make the wrong answer more confident.

The confusion is between a rare term and a rare substring. 18 is rare because numbers are fragments of larger numbers, not because it carries meaning. A tokenizer that treats digits as units of evidence is measuring typography, not language. Same reason 8 and 800 and 1800 all look like unrelated, highly specific facts.

The gate: does the query still contain a subject?

I stopped trying to make the score smarter and put a check in front of it instead. Strip the units, the dimension words, the numerals and the question particles. If nothing is left, the query is not a document lookup — it is a parameter lookup, and a search box has no business answering it.

var MEASURE = /米|厘米|毫米|公分|吨|公斤|千克|kg|mm|cm|多高|多宽|多长|多重|多厚|多少|几个|几根|几块|几米|[0-9.\s]/g;

function hasSignal(raw) {
  var t = raw.replace(MEASURE, "").replace(/高|宽|长|厚|重|大|小|的/g, "");
  // a CJK noun survived, or an identifier like hrb400 / c30 / pavement
  return /[\u4e00-\u9fff]/.test(t) || /[a-z]{2,}/.test(t);
}

Two details matter. The strip list is deliberately greedy — 高宽长厚重 are the words people use to describe a dimension, and leaving them in would let 18米高 pass as a subject. The second clause keeps real identifiers alive: hrb400 and c30 are not measurements, and killing them would break every steel and concrete query on the site.

When the gate returns false, the fallback does not run, and the UI says nothing was found and offers the category list. Zero results beats a plausible wrong one, because the two failures have different costs. Someone who gets nothing retypes the query. Someone who gets a hook-length table concludes the site doesn't have a scaffolding calculator and leaves.

Measured, before and after

Twenty dimension-only queries — 18米高8米宽, 6米跨度, 4.5米层高, 300高, 0.5米厚, and so on — run against the same 238-card index, with the old fallback and the gated one:

Answered Relevant
Old fallback 19 / 20 0 / 19
Gated 3 / 20 0 / 3

Nineteen out of twenty got an answer, and not one of them was about the right thing. That is the shape of the bug: not a rare wrong answer, but a system that answered almost everything and was almost never right.

I'll be straight about the residual. Three still get through, because 跨度 and 层高 are genuine nouns even though the query is a dimension: 6米跨度 returns four cards, 4.5米层高 returns two (paint coverage and wallpaper, both of which mention ceiling height in passing). And 18米高8米宽间距1.5 returns fourteen, because 间距 survives the strip — it is a real word, and it is also the one word in that sentence that describes a parameter rather than a product. A vocabulary of parameter nouns would fix those. I haven't built it, and I'd rather ship the gate that removes 16 wrong answers than wait for the one that removes 19.

The second-order cost, in the analytics

Every search reports its result count. Zero-result queries are the useful ones: a demand list of things people asked for that the site doesn't have, which I read every morning.

For as long as the fallback answered these queries, they never appeared as misses. The 18 × 8 m scaffold, the 6 m span, the wall thickness — all recorded as successful searches. The bug didn't just serve the wrong page; it deleted the evidence that the page was missing. Two weeks of demand data, silently scored 1.00.

That is the part I'd flag to anyone with a hand-rolled matcher: a false positive in search is also a false negative in your product backlog, and only one of those is visible to the user.

Reproducing it

The harness reads the built index.html, pulls every card's data-k, and runs both versions of the fallback against the same 20 queries:

score = sum(1 for g in valid if g in key) / len(valid)   # identical to the JS
if max_score >= 0.5: winners = [c for c in cards if s(c) >= max_score - 1e-9]

Run it against your own index and look at two numbers: how many cards tie at the maximum, and how many of the query's surviving grams are digits or fragments of digits. If both are non-zero, your fallback is answering questions it cannot read.

The site this came from is jianzhujisuan.com, a set of construction-quantity calculators with 238 tools on the index. The scaffolding page is the one that visitor was actually looking for, and it took a comment-section bug report for the search box to stop hiding it.

The lesson I keep re-learning, in one line: a relevance score is a claim about the query, not about the page. Mine was computed entirely from the page, and so it was 1.00 on a query that had nothing in it to be relevant to.

articles.title: I Haven't Written a Line of Code in Months. And I Don't Know How to Feel About It.
articles.description: Introduction   It's been a while since I wrote something here. It feels like it was a...
articles.body_html:
Introduction

It's been a while since I wrote something here. It feels like it was a lifetime ago. Our world, and especially our programming world, moves so fast that I can't recognize the way it was 6 years ago, 2 years ago, or even at the beginning of this year. So, I wanted to write down some thoughts and see where they take me.

Dealing with changes

In our line of work, we're used to changes right? New languages, new technologies, new frameworks... we've always had new things to look forward to, or being scared of, learn, hate... But this AI stuff... Damn, it's not just something new, it's the first time I've actually felt threatened, in danger, overwhelmed.

It's a very strange feeling because I have the feeling like we are at the edge of a new world, full of possibilities, adventures, discoveries. Things that we thought would take us weeks, months, or years to do or solve become doable so much faster. In the field of science, we see cool stuff happening. And even if I don't understand anything about it, it looks cool to discover new proofs and solutions, even if it's AI assisted. But...

What about me?

I'm a good developer ok? I'm not a rockstar, but I've some strenghts. I've always enjoyed learning new stuff about design patterns, how to write good code. Less than a year ago, I was still learning new things, trying to write more elegant code. I was happy when I found a beautiful solution to a problem.

Around March this year, our team decided it was time to equip everyone with Claude. I don't think I've written a line of code since then. How insane is that? Most of my time was spent in writing code, and now, it has completely disappeared from my tasks. So now, I'm mostly managing agents and doing all the conception and planning. That's where my "expertise" comes in. Because this stuff writes much better code than me anyway.

I feel... dizzy.

What about my (our) future?

The one thing that is scary is not knowing to me. I don't know what our jobs will look like next year, in 2 years, in 10 years. Will we still have a job? How will it look? I'm not much into the doom prediction like "Developers will be gone in 6 months". But something is gonna change drastically right? What about the juniors, the people entering the job market today?

It's not all bad of course. It's not. It's the uncertainty that's difficult for me.

I'm building a very cool project with a few colleagues and AI allowed us to move a lot faster than we would have on our own. That's really exciting. Being able to deliver features a lot faster to users is always a nice feeling. That's one of the main reasons I started doing this anyway, help people.

Loss of craftsmanship

When I wrote the code, with my slow hands, I felt like a craftsman. I was building something. The code was mine. Now, it's not. It's industrialized. A machine makes it. Like countless other craftsmen in the history of our species, what I used to do with my hands in hours or days is done by a machine in minutes.

It's a strange feeling. Of course, I try to comfort myself. I still need to pilot this thing. It doesn't have my humanity, it doesn't know my users like I know them. I have better business knowledge than this machine. And in the end, it's always me that makes the final decision. For how long? And how much value does it have?

This is also why I write this. Because I can still sit in front of my computer and pour out the words. My words. From my brain and my heart. It feels good to create something all by yourself. And I still have the hope that whatever the future holds for us, we will build cool stuff to help people. I hope that the AI era that we're entering will be a net positive for humanity.

Conclusion

That's it, that was my little rant. I'll keep building things that I believe will help people to better their lives and jobs. We will see, together, where this new world takes us.

Have fun <3

articles.description: Introduction   In this article, I'll expose an issue we had in one of my freelance missions,...
