articles.title: The Provider Said 'Already Charged'. Nothing Was Charged.
articles.description: Saturday morning, before coffee, a customer called Ana wrote in. She had tried to buy the $29 book...
articles.body_html:
Saturday morning, before coffee, a customer called Ana wrote in. She had tried to buy the $29 book twice, and twice my site told her she had already paid. Her bank showed nothing, and no order existed on my side. She asked whether I had taken her money and forgotten the book. I had not taken anything. My checkout had refused her money and then told her the refusal was her own history.

That email is the whole piece. A provider saying "already charged" is a rumour, not a receipt, and most payment code treats it as a verdict. It should not. On a first attempt the provider's word can be wrong in the direction nobody checks for: it can say the money moved when nothing moved at all. If your code believes it, you do something quieter than double-charging anyone. You turn away a customer who is trying to pay you, and no statement, no dashboard, no alert ever shows you did it.

ilragioniere put this to me in the comments, and he put it better than I could. He called it the false positive, and the quietest failure in the whole series: a provider that answers "already charged" when nothing was charged skips a real charge forever, and no statement ever shows it. His floor under it: the provider's own settlement report, a charge record nobody prunes, dated, independent of the key. Inside the lag, answer "unknown, hold" and let the file settle it when it lands. So I ran his shape. I built a small stand-in for the provider, one that lies on purpose, and I put two ways of handling a first attempt through the same 10 tries, twice over.

The stand-in answers "already charged" on every first attempt, even when no charge exists and no settlement line exists. That is the lie, stated plainly. The first handler is the three-line version: if the provider says already charged, skip. It never looks at the settlement file. The second handler reads the provider's answer and refuses to trust it. It says "unknown, hold", waits for the settlement file to land, and reads that instead. No line in the file means no settlement, and the charge goes ahead. A matching line means the charge is real, and nothing is charged twice.

The count is what makes this more than an opinion. Across 60 first attempts the stand-in said "already charged" 60 times, and in all 60 nothing had been charged. The trusting handler skipped 20 out of 20 real charges, $580 of payments refused, and never once looked at the file. The careful handler charged 20 out of 20 when the file held no matching line, $580 taken properly, and recognised the charge 20 out of 20 times when the file did hold one, with zero second charges. Same lie, same tries. The only difference was what each handler treated as evidence.

Five things I took away from that count.

  1. The lie leaves no trace. A double charge is loud. The customer sees $58 for a $29 book and asks for a refund. A skipped charge is silent. The provider took nothing, the file lists nothing, and the only record of the missing money is a customer deciding whether to write in or just leave. Ana wrote in. Most people do not; they assume the site is broken and buy the book somewhere else. Your numbers stay clean while sales quietly shrink, and nothing in your records can tell you why.

  2. The two mistakes are not the same size. A false "not charged" costs a double charge, a refund, and a thread with an unhappy customer. Somebody sees it the same day. A false "already charged" costs one charge nobody sees, found only if a customer complains. The loud error gets the guardrails and the late-night fixes. The quiet one gets trusted code and a shrug, because nobody has felt it yet. That is exactly backwards. The error you cannot see is the one you have to design against, not the one you will notice.

  3. The key cannot rescue this one. The key is a good tool for the job it does. If the charge landed and your own record of it did not, the key stops the retry from charging twice. But this failure happens before any of that. It is a first attempt. Nothing was charged, so there is no key entry worth asking about, and if the key was pruned it is gone anyway. A key proves a retry is the same request. It was never a receipt.

  4. The search lags, and the lag has a floor. The other place people look is the charge search: ask by your own order number instead of by key. It beats the key, and the previous piece showed it surviving a pruned key. But a search is not a read. It lags the charge by seconds, and inside those seconds the only honest answer is that you do not know yet. Code that cannot say "I don't know" fills the gap with whatever answer arrives first, usually the provider's confident one. The floor under the lag is the file: the settlement report lands on its own schedule, dated, and once it lands it does not change its mind.

  5. The file is the only thing nobody prunes. Keys get pruned, searches lag. The settlement file is the provider's own record of money that actually moved, written down after the fact, and it answers a different question from the other two: not "do you remember this request" but "did this money move". With the line absent, the careful handler's answer was not "already charged" but "no settlement", with the age of the attempt attached, and then it charged. With the line present, it said charged, and it was right. It is not fast or convenient. It is the one record that does not depend on the answer you are trying to check.

There is a limit to what this run can claim, and I would rather state it plainly. The provider here is a stand-in I built, not a real payment company, and the settlement file is one I wrote myself, landing a second after each attempt. The shape of the lie is real and the counts are real, but a real provider's file could arrive late, mangled, or not at all, and I did not measure that. The check that would close this properly needs a real sandbox account, a real charge, a pruned key, and both answers held up against the settlement line. I have not done that one, and I am not going to pretend the stand-in is the same thing. What it does prove is narrower: the three-line shortcut fails every time the provider is wrong, and the hold-and-read shape survives the same lie in both directions, twenty times out of twenty.

So here is where I land. Never let a provider's "already charged" be the last word on whether money moved. Read it, then check the record that does not depend on it. Inside the lag, say you do not know, wait for the file, and let the file decide. It costs a second and one extra read per attempt. The alternative costs customers you will never hear from, which is a strange price to pay for saving a second.

Has this one bitten you? As a buyer, were you ever told you had already paid when your bank said otherwise, and what did you do, write in or walk away? As a builder, what do you check first when a charge is in doubt, the provider's answer or your own records, and has the provider's answer ever been wrong for you? Tell me what you found. The quiet failures are the ones I only hear about when somebody says so out loud.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

articles.title: The Guardrails I Give My AI Coding Agent
articles.description: In my last post I wrote that the more I use AI to code, the more engineering judgment matters. A fair...
articles.body_html:
In my last post I wrote that the more I use AI to code, the more engineering judgment matters. A fair follow-up question is: what does that judgment look like on an ordinary day?

For the past few weeks, an AI coding agent (Claude Code, in my case) has been writing much of the code for our product's search pages. In one day this week it shipped four separate changes to our development environment: a new way to combine filters with a plain-text view of a search, two small visual fixes, and a layout change for smaller laptop screens.

I didn't write those changes. I did decide what got built, what shipped and what "done" meant.

Those decisions are what I want to describe. Most of them are not clever. They are guardrails: rules the agent follows every time, so that speed doesn't turn into surprises.

1. Two decisions stay with me: build it, and ship it

The agent can investigate, propose and build. When it finishes an investigation, it gives me a recommendation rather than a list of every possible option, and then it waits. My answer is usually short: "Yes, build it."

When the change is built and checked, it stops again and asks whether to ship. "Yes, ship it" is a separate decision, and it is mine.

Splitting the two matters more than it sounds. The first approval is about the idea. The second is about the result, after I have seen it. Without the second stop, approving an idea quietly turns into approving whatever came out.

2. Show me, don't tell me

A description of a UI change is not evidence. Every visual change goes onto a local preview first, and the agent sends me screenshots before anything is pushed.

Take the layout change from this week. On a smaller laptop, the panel beside our search form pushed its main buttons, View Results and Download, below the edge of the screen. The fix keeps the count at the top and the buttons at the bottom, and lets only the details between them scroll.

The agent didn't stop at "it works on my screen". It checked:

  • 1366 x 640, a common short laptop window: the buttons end 24 pixels above the bottom edge.
  • 1366 x 560, a very short window: still visible.
  • 1440 x 1000: nothing scrolls, so nothing should look different, and nothing did.
  • Tablet and phone widths, where the page uses a different layout altogether.

At each size it also ran a small script that looks for anything spilling sideways out of its container, the kind of overflow that is easy to miss at a glance.

If you take one habit from this post, take this one: decide which screen sizes count, and make "checked at those sizes, with screenshots" part of done.

3. Merge only on green, and only the commit that was tested

The agent opens a pull request and waits for CI. It merges only when every check is green, and it pins the merge to the exact commit the checks ran against:

gh pr checks "$PR" --watch --fail-fast
gh pr merge "$PR" --merge --match-head-commit "$HEAD_SHA"

--match-head-commit makes the merge fail if anything was pushed to the branch after the checks started. Without it, "CI was green" can describe a different commit from the one that lands.

A red check is never something to talk around. Either the code gets fixed, or the agent explains why the test itself is out of date, changes it in the open and says so in the pull request. It does not quietly loosen a test to get to green.

4. Tests that pin the rules people forget

Some of my favourite tests are almost embarrassingly simple. They read a source file as text and check it with a regular expression:

import test from 'node:test';
import assert from 'node:assert/strict';
import fs from 'node:fs';

const css = fs.readFileSync('resources/css/search.css', 'utf8');

test('colours come from design tokens, never hex values', () => {
  assert.doesNotMatch(css, /#[0-9a-fA-F]{3,8}\b/);
});

A test like this caught the agent this week. To fade the edges of the new scrolling area, it used a CSS mask with #000 in the gradient. The colour never even shows (a mask only uses transparency), but the rule is the rule, and the test failed. The fix took seconds: black instead of #000. What matters is that I didn't have to notice it.

We have tests like this for:

  • no em dashes or curly quotes in customer-facing text (a single curly apostrophe in a release note failed the tests once, which is exactly what I wanted);
  • a maximum length for release note titles and summaries;
  • a line limit on one large component, which pushes new logic into its own file instead of growing one file forever.

None of these rules are hard to check. They are hard to remember, especially at the speed an agent works. A rule that lives only in a style guide will be broken eventually. A rule that lives in a test is checked every time.

5. Every change ships with its own story

Each user-facing change includes two pieces of writing in the same pull request:

  • a short "What's New" entry that customers see in the product, with a title under 70 characters and a summary under 260;
  • a line in our internal product document saying what changed, why, who asked for it and where the code lives.

The agent writes both. It knows the change better than anyone at that moment, so this is the cheapest time to write it down. Because it happens in the same pull request, the documentation never falls a release behind, and tests hold the customer-facing text to its length and style limits.

6. Check it where it lives, and leave it as you found it

Green CI and a good local preview are not the end. After each deploy, the agent opens the change on our development environment and checks it again, using my own saved search as the test case.

That comes with firm limits:

  • It never touches production.
  • It never signs in as me. If the session has expired, it tells me and waits.
  • On the development environment it reads, and avoids changing real records or running expensive exports.
  • When it has to change something to test it, such as a draft search, it saves the original first and puts it back afterwards.

The last point matters more than it seems. A test environment that slowly fills up with leftovers from automated checks stops being trustworthy.

7. Write the traps down

Every project has traps that cost an afternoon the first time. The agent keeps a notes file of them and reads it at the start of every session.

One example from our search: when the agent set up a test search using a field's internal sample name instead of its real name, the filter still appeared on screen, but the search silently ignored it. The count looked plausible and was wrong. That trap is now one line in the notes, with the rule that goes with it: always use the live field name.

The format doesn't matter much. What matters is that a lesson learned once isn't paid for again in the next session.

8. Small, boring commits

A few habits keep the history easy to read and easy to undo:

  • One change per pull request, even on a day with four of them.
  • Files are staged by name, never with a blanket git add, so scratch files and stray experiments don't ride along.
  • Commit messages say what changed for the user, not only what changed in the code.

If something goes wrong, I want to point at one small pull request and revert it without unpicking three other things.

What the guardrails are really for

None of this slows the agent down much. Most of it is automated, and the rest is two short answers from me. What it changes is what I am responsible for.

I don't need to read every line at the speed it was written. I need to be confident about the things that matter: what the change does, that it was tested at the sizes and in the situations we care about, that it follows our rules, and that what was tested is what shipped. The guardrails turn those from things I hope are true into things that are checked.

In my last post I said that if I ship something, I need to be able to explain it, debug it and maintain it. These guardrails are a large part of how I keep that promise while an agent does most of the typing.

What guardrails have you put around AI-written code? I'd especially like to hear about cheap checks that have caught real mistakes.

articles.title: The Comment That Ruined My Thursday
articles.description: 09:12. I open the pull request and there it is, three words under a line of my code, in red.  "This...
articles.body_html:
09:12. I open the pull request and there it is, three words under a line of my code, in red.

"This is wrong."

No line number beyond the one it sits on. No "because". No "try this instead". Just the three words, and a name beside them I recognise from the team list, and a little grey timestamp that says it arrived at 08:47, twenty-five minutes before I got to my desk.

I read it again. Then I read it a third time, slower, as if the extra words might be hiding between the three that are there. They are not.

The line it sits on is mine. It sorts a list of invoices by date, and I wrote it on Tuesday afternoon, in a hurry, because the dashboard needed it and the afternoon was already gone. I remember writing it. I remember feeling clever about it for about four seconds, which is the usual length of time I feel clever about anything I write.

09:14. I click on the file. The function is eleven lines long. I read it the way you read a text from someone you like, looking for the tone underneath the words. It sorts. It returns. It handles the empty list. I check the tests. Two tests, both green, both mine. I run them again anyway, because running them feels like doing something, and they go green again, which tells me nothing except that the tests agree with me, and the tests were written by me, so of course they agree with me.

09:31. I start a reply.

"Could you say a bit more about what's wrong here? Happy to fix it."

I read it back. It sounds fine. It sounds like a person who is not bothered at all. I delete it. It sounds too fine, which is the problem. If I send that, I will spend the rest of the day wondering whether she thinks I am being passive-aggressive, and she will spend the rest of the day wondering whether I am. Nobody wins.

09:47. Second draft.

"Which part is wrong? The sort, or the date handling?"

Shorter. Honest. I hover over the button. My finger does not press it. Because what if she answers "both", and then I have to ask again, and now I am the person who needs three rounds of comments to understand one line of code. I delete it too.

10:05. Third draft, and this one is long. It explains why I wrote it this way. It mentions the Tuesday deadline. It points out that the tests pass. It has a paragraph about the date format coming in as a string from the old system, which is true, and which has nothing to do with anything. I read the whole thing and I can hear how it sounds: a man building a small fort out of excuses and sitting inside it. I select all of it and delete it, and the empty box looks back at me, and I feel better and worse at the same time.

10:40. I give up on the reply and go back to the code. This is the part of the day where I become a detective in my own flat, looking for something I lost in a room I cleaned myself.

Maybe it is the sort. The dates arrive as strings, "2026-11-04", "2026-11-19", and string sort works fine on those, until it doesn't. I think about it. It works fine. I think about it more. It still works fine. I think about it until "works fine" starts to sound like something a person says right before finding out it doesn't.

Maybe it is the empty list. Maybe it is the duplicate dates. Maybe it is the fact that I named the variable sorted and shadowed something somewhere. I open the file that calls this function. I open the file that calls that file. By 11:20 I have five tabs open and I am reading code I wrote last month as if it were written by a stranger who might have left me a clue.

11:58. I close the tabs. I have found three things that might be wrong, and I am not sure about any of them, and the honest truth is that I could rewrite the whole function in twenty minutes and still not know whether I fixed the thing she meant. I eat lunch at my desk, which I never do, because leaving the desk feels like leaving the argument, and the argument is only happening in my head, and I cannot leave my head.

13:20. I check the thread. Nothing new. The three words are still there, patient as a parked car. I read them again and this time I notice the full stop. "This is wrong." The full stop makes it worse. Without it, it could be a thought she typed quickly. With it, it sounds finished. Settled. A verdict with nowhere to go.

13:44. I open the reply box again. I type "Thanks for catching this —" and stop. Thanks for catching what? I do not know what she caught. I am thanking her for a mystery. I delete it.

14:15. I do actual work for an hour, or I pretend to. I fix a typo in a readme. I rename a variable in a file nobody will ever open. I answer two messages with unusual speed, because answering messages is a thing I can complete, and the comment is a thing I cannot. Every ten minutes I click back to the pull request, the way you check a phone that has not buzzed, and every time the thread is the same, and every time I am a little annoyed at myself for checking.

15:30. I write the reply I should have written at 09:14. Six words.

"What part is wrong? Happy to fix."

No explanation, no defence, no "thanks for catching this". Just the question, asked plainly, the way I would ask it if she were sitting next to me and I had not spent six hours making it complicated. I press the button before I can re-read it. The page reloads. My question sits under her comment, small and a little bit naked, and there is nothing to do now except wait, which turns out to be its own kind of work.

16:02. She is online. I can see the little dot. I watch the dot the way you watch a kettle. The dot stays. Nothing arrives. I open another file and stare at it without reading it.

16:41. The reply comes. Two lines.

"The sort compares the strings, so the 9th sorts after the 19th. Compare the timestamps instead."

I read it twice. Then I laugh, out loud, alone, at my desk, because of course. Of course it is the dates. The strings sort fine until the day number hits double digits and then "9" sits after "19" like it owns the place, and every invoice from the first nine days of the month has been sitting in the wrong order for a week, and the tests passed because both my test dates were in the twenties. A four-minute fix. A four-minute fix that cost me a Thursday.

16:47. I change one line. I compare the timestamps. I run the tests. Green. I add a third test with a date on the 9th and a date on the 19th, because that is the test I should have written on Tuesday, and it goes red before the fix and green after, which is the sound a test is supposed to make. I push. I write "Fixed — sorting by timestamp now, added a test for single-digit days." I press the button. The thread closes itself in my head the way a door closes when you finally stop holding it open.

17:20. The rest of the day is quiet. The quiet is the strange part. The comment is answered, the code is fixed, and there is nothing left to be angry about, which leaves me with the anger and nowhere to put it. I keep thinking about the six hours. Not the bug. The bug was four minutes. The six hours were mine. I spent them writing replies I never sent and reading code I had already read, because three words with no "because" felt like a verdict, and I treated it like one, and a verdict is something you defend yourself against, and a question is something you just answer.

18:35. A pull request from someone else lands in my queue. A new joiner, three weeks in, and I open it, and I read it, and I find the thing that is wrong. It is a small thing. A loop that runs one time too many. I click on the line. The comment box opens, empty and patient. I type "this is wrong" and I look at it, sitting there in the box, three words and a full stop, and I delete it.

I write the other version instead. The line number, and what it does wrong, and what to change, and the two minutes it will take. I read it back and it sounds like a person who wants the code fixed, not a person who wants to be right. I press the button. The comment goes out with my name beside it, and the thread waits, and somewhere on the other side of it a person is about to have a much shorter Thursday than I did.

P.S. Everything I write stays free — that part doesn't change. But if this one was worth something to you, you can buy me a coffee ☕ (one-time or monthly, both work). It covers the API credits and hosting behind these experiments — and honestly, it's also the nudge that gets the next one started on the evenings I'd otherwise skip it. — Salam

articles.title: My --config-test accepted a listen address that could never bind
articles.description: transponder is a Go proxy I've been building. It has a --config-test flag: load the config, validate...
articles.body_html:
transponder is a Go proxy I've been building. It has a --config-test flag: load the config, validate it, exit 0 or 1. It runs in CI and in the deploy script before anything starts.

Last week a config passed --config-test and the server died 200 ms later with:

listen tcp: lookup tcp/nope: unknown port

No key name, no line number, nothing to grep for. The config had listen_addr: ":nope".

The check I wrote

Validation did the obvious thing: net.SplitHostPort, then strconv.Atoi and a range check. It felt correct because the standard library was doing the parsing.

SplitHostPort is a splitter, not a validator. Here it is against the values that kill net.Listen (Go 1.27.1, on this box):

SplitHostPort(":")             = "",          "",      <nil>
SplitHostPort(":nope")         = "",          "nope",  <nil>
SplitHostPort(":70000")        = "",          "70000", <nil>
SplitHostPort("localhost:+80") = "localhost", "+80",   <nil>

Every one splits fine. net.Listen disagrees with some of them:

:nope    -> listen tcp: lookup tcp/nope: unknown port
:70000   -> listen tcp: address 70000: invalid port
:        -> ok on [::]:39331
:+0      -> ok on [::]:44017

: — the value that looks most broken — binds a free port quite happily. And :+0 binds too: signed ports are legal, which I had assumed they weren't. So the port has to be read the way net.Listen reads it — a number in 0–65535, or a service name resolved through net.LookupPort — and not with whatever cut the string.

func splitListenAddr(key, addr string) (host string, port int, err error) {
    rawHost, rawPort, err := net.SplitHostPort(addr)
    if err != nil || rawPort == "" {
        return "", 0, fmt.Errorf("config: %s %q must be host:port, such as :8080", key, addr)
    }
    if n, err := strconv.Atoi(rawPort); err == nil {
        if n < 0 || n > 65535 {
            return "", 0, fmt.Errorf("config: %s %q has the port %q, which must be between 0 and 65535", key, addr, rawPort)
        }
        return rawHost, n, nil
    }
    n, err := net.LookupPort("tcp", rawPort)
    if err != nil {
        return "", 0, fmt.Errorf("config: %s %q names the port %q, which is neither a number nor a known service", key, addr, rawPort)
    }
    return rawHost, n, nil
}

No socket opened, no DNS. LookupPort reads the local service list, which is the same list net.Listen would read.

Then the two-listener case

The service has a main listener and an ops listener. The same port on both is a startup failure, so the config check compares them — except when either port is 0, which asks the kernel for a free one.

Comparing hosts is net.IP.Equal plus case folding, with a zone split off first because net.ParseIP doesn't read zones. Fine. Then I wrote the wildcard rule: an unspecified address reaches everything, so refuse it next to any host on the same port.

CodeRabbit said I had that backwards for 0.0.0.0 next to [::1]. I said no — they bind separately, the v4 wildcard is v4.

They were right, and it took one command:

$ go run .   # listen on 0.0.0.0:42771, then [::1]:42771
[::1]:42771 -> listen tcp [::1]:42771: bind: address already in use

Go's favoriteAddrFamily opens an IPv4 wildcard as a dual-stack AF_INET6 socket, so 0.0.0.0 claims the v6 side as well. ss -lnt6 lists it, ss -lnt4 doesn't. My mental model came from C, not from net/ipsock_posix.go.

What shipped is the conservative rule: any unspecified host conflicts with anything on that port. On a platform that binds the v4 wildcard v4-only, that refuses a pair which would have worked — and a config that passes and then can't start is exactly the bug the check exists to catch.

Zones are the same story

net.ParseIP ignores zones, so fe80::1%eth0 and fe80::1%eth1 compare equal and a real collision between two interfaces slips through. Split on the first %, compare address and zone separately, and refuse what net.Listen refuses:

127.0.0.1%lo:0      -> lookup 127.0.0.1%lo: no such host   (v4 takes no zone)
[fe80::1%]:0        -> lookup fe80::1%: no such host       (empty zone)
[fe80::1%eth0%x]:0  -> bind: invalid argument              (second %)

The rule

A config check earns its keep only if it reads each value the way the consumer reads it. Same parser, same edge cases, same refusals — or explicit, documented strictness where reproducing the consumer is impossible. Anything else is a linter wearing a --config-test sticker: it approves the file, the process dies anyway, and the error arrives without the key that caused it.

Eighty lines and two test tables to move one class of startup failure from 11pm to CI. Worth it. The patch is #206 on raven-clown/transponder if you want to read the reject cases.

articles.title: Interaction Nets Explained: The Programming Model Behind the Frostbite CPU
articles.description: On November 18, 2026, the chip-design startup Architect Labs published a post introducing Frostbite....
articles.body_html:
On November 18, 2026, the chip-design startup Architect Labs published a post introducing Frostbite. They describe it as a general-purpose CPU with a new instruction set. They say their AI systems designed it, from the compiler down to the final chip layout. The Hacker News thread reached 657 points and 342 comments.

Most coverage is about the AI and the headline number: 4.59x better performance per watt than a conventional core. This article looks at the part software developers can try today. Frostbite runs programs as interaction nets, a model of computation that is more than 35 years old. The language that compiles to it, Vine, is open source, and you can install it with Cargo today.

A note on sources: I have not run Vine or seen Frostbite hardware. Every number below comes from the linked sources: the Frostbite post, the Vine documentation, an explainer from the company behind Vine, and the HN discussion.

What Frostbite claims, in short

All of these come from the Architect Labs post:

  • The workloads. 25 programs in five groups: parallel, staged, sequential, branching, and recursive. The agents tuned the design on 10 of them. The other 15 were held out until the final evaluation.
  • The headline result. One Frostbite "quad" (a two-by-two group of tiles) reached a geometric mean of 4.59x the performance per watt of the comparison core across all 25 workloads. That splits into 6.02x on the 10 tuning workloads and 3.83x on the 15 held-out ones.
  • Area. An average 8.77x performance per area, on a 7 nm process.
  • The baseline. The comparison core is "a modern, silicon-proven superscalar (dual-issue, in-order) CPU core". A footnote says: "For legal reasons, we cannot disclose the exact CPU."
  • The status. The design reached 500 MHz in the final GDS (the layout file sent to a chip factory). The post itself calls the power numbers "pre-silicon". It does not report results from a manufactured chip.
  • The process. The specification ended as formal contracts that compiled to more than 800,000 lines of Lean (a proof assistant). The agents tried 58 design ideas and kept 37.

Why can this design drop so much of a normal CPU's hardware? The answer is in the programming model.

Why your CPU spends energy guessing

A normal compiler sees which operations in your program depend on each other. It uses that information for optimization. Then it throws most of it away and produces one long list of instructions.

The CPU then tries to rebuild that information at runtime. Out-of-order cores keep large buffers to find instructions that can run early. Multicore chips add cache coherence protocols so every core sees the same memory, because any instruction might touch any address.

The explainer from Tendrils, the company that develops Vine, puts it this way: "Normal compilers already track these dependencies internally and use them to make optimizations. However, this information is then thrown away and the entire program is linearized into a sequence of instructions."

Frostbite's post shows the cost. Leaving out clock distribution, the comparison core spends 57% of its energy on memory and 27% on fetching, decoding, and issuing instructions. Only 13% goes to computing. Interaction nets keep the dependency information instead.

Interaction nets in four ideas

Interaction nets were introduced by Yves Lafont in a 1990 paper at POPL, a major programming-languages conference. The model fits in four ideas.

1. A program is a graph of nodes. Each node has exactly one principal port (its main connection point) and zero or more auxiliary ports (extra connection points). Wires connect ports. In the simple examples, a number and an addition are both nodes.

2. Computation is rewriting pairs. When a wire connects the principal ports of two nodes, they form an active pair. A rule says how that pair is replaced by a small new piece of graph. Then the next active pair is rewritten, and so on, until none are left. Each step only touches the two nodes involved. Tendrils calls this property locality.

3. Active pairs never overlap. A node has only one principal port, so it can be part of only one active pair at a time. That means all active pairs are independent. You can rewrite them in any order, or all at once, and the final result is the same. This property is called confluence. In practice it means no race conditions: there is no shared variable for two threads to fight over.

4. Every value is used exactly once. This is linearity. If a value needs to be used twice, the net contains an explicit duplicate node. If it is not used, an explicit erase node destroys it. Nothing is copied or dropped by accident. Rust developers will recognize the idea: it is close to ownership.

The Tendrils explainer shows this with unary arithmetic. In its multiplication example, the first rewrite leaves two independent active pairs, which can run in parallel with no coordination. Nobody added that parallelism. It is a side effect of keeping the dependencies.

What linearity looks like in Vine

Nobody wants to wire graph nodes by hand. Vine is a language with syntax close to Rust that compiles to interaction nets. Its Apache-2.0 GitHub repository calls it "an experimental new programming language based on interaction nets". Vine compiles to Ivy, a low-level net language, which runs on a runtime called the IVM. The Frostbite post says programs for the chip are written in Vine and compiled to Ivy.

Linearity shows up in Vine's type system as "flexibility". The Fork and Drop documentation says every type has two yes-or-no properties: can its values be forked (copied), and can they be dropped (destroyed)? The annotations work like regex quantifiers:

  • No annotation: values must be used exactly once.
  • ?: values may be used zero or one times (droppable).
  • +: values may be used one or more times (forkable).
  • *: values may be used zero or more times (both).

When you use a variable twice, the compiler inserts a fork for you. The docs show (used_multiple_times, used_multiple_times) becoming (used_multiple_times.fork(), used_multiple_times) behind the scenes.

The IO type cannot be forked or dropped. The docs explain the result: "at any point in the execution of a Vine program, there is exactly one IO handle, so all IO operations are ordered." So the language gets ordered side effects from the type system, while pure computation stays free to run in parallel.

Measure your program's parallelism with one flag

Vine can tell you how parallel a program is, without any parallel hardware.

The installation page needs Rust and one command:

cargo install --git https://github.com/VineLang/vine --locked

Every Vine program needs a main function that takes the IO handle. The hello world is:

pub fn main(&io: &IO) {
  io.println("Hello, world!");
}

Run it with vine run hello_world.vi. After the output, Vine prints statistics. The docs show 341 total interactions for this program. The statistics page says the total interaction count is deterministic: "the same program will always have the exact same interaction count, no matter what machine it is run on." That makes it a stable measure of work, unlike wall-clock time.

The useful flag is --breadth-first. The CLI docs say it runs the program so that "at each step, every possible interaction is performed in parallel." This pretends you have a machine with unlimited cores. It reports three numbers:

  • Total: all interactions, the amount of work.
  • Depth: the number of parallel steps needed. This is the critical path, the longest chain of steps that must happen one after another.
  • Breadth: total divided by depth, the average number of interactions ready at each step.

This is the work-span model from algorithms courses: total is the work, depth is the span, and breadth is the average parallelism.

A worked example: longest common subsequence

The Tendrils explainer uses the longest common subsequence problem. Given two lists, find the length of the longest sequence of items that appears in both, in order, but not always next to each other. For "Tendrils" and "edits", the answer is "edis", length 4.

Here is their Vine code, a plain dynamic-programming version with two nested loops and no parallel hints:

pub fn lcs[T*; Eq[T]](a: List[T], b: List[T]) -> N32 {
  let row = [];
  for a_elem in a {
    let prev_row_entry = 0;
    let prev_new_entry = 0;
    let new_row = [];
    for b_elem in b {
      let row_entry = row.pop_front().or_use(0);
      let new_entry = if a_elem == b_elem {
        prev_row_entry + 1
      } else {
        row_entry.max(prev_new_entry)
      };
      prev_row_entry = row_entry;
      prev_new_entry = new_entry;
      new_row.push_back(new_entry);
    }
    row = new_row;
  }

  row.get(b.len() - 1).or_use(0)
}

Note the T* in the signature. With the flexibility rules above, that says list items may be copied or dropped freely.

They ran it on two random lists of 200 items with vine run lcs.vi --breadth-first:

Interactions
  Total            2_993_893
    Depth             10_920
    Breadth              274

On average, 274 interactions could run at each step. Then they increased both lists to 2,000 items:

Interactions
  Total          296_223_905
    Depth            108_142
    Breadth            2_739

The total work grew about 100x, because the algorithm is quadratic. The depth grew only about 10x. The explainer gives the reason: every cell on a diagonal of the DP table is independent of the others, so the critical path is just the main diagonal, which grows linearly. The parallel work grows with the input.

The explainer says the Vine compiler does this "not by magically extracting parallelism out of the program; it simply preserves dependency information all the way down to the hardware (or runtime, in this case)."

Frostbite's post shows the same pattern on a smaller problem. For five queens on a five-by-five board, the net runs 3,183 interactions with a critical path of 262 steps. On average, about twelve interactions are ready at every step.

How to read your own numbers

If you try this on your own algorithms, keep two limits in mind:

  • Breadth-first mode is optimistic. The CLI docs say it "gives an upper bound on the speedup that could be seen from a parallel machine." Real hardware has a fixed number of cores and pays to move work between them.
  • Depth is the floor. No hardware can finish faster than the critical path. A program with a breadth near 1 is sequential, whatever the chip is. This is close to Amdahl's law, and one HN commenter made that point about general-purpose code: "the longest serial task is what ends up slowing everything down."

From a net to a chip: how Frostbite schedules work

Frostbite is a grid of tiles. Each tile has a small local memory, an engine, and a runtime block. Because every value has one owner and every step is local, data can sit in small memories next to where it is used, instead of in a deep shared cache.

There is no central scheduler. The Frostbite post says each tile follows three rules:

  1. Run your own work first (the work in your input ports).
  2. If you have none, take work from a neighboring tile that has some to spare.
  3. If no neighbor has any, go inactive and save power.

Per the post, when a loop or branch splits into parallel pieces, the running code parks what comes next in a small record (the "frame manager"), puts the new tasks on a hardware "work queue", and takes the newest one itself. Idle neighbors pull the rest over the on-chip network. When the last piece returns, the parked code wakes up.

The post calls this "stealing work". Java developers know the same idea from ForkJoinPool, which its docs describe as "employing work-stealing". Here it is built into the tile hardware. The post says no human specified it and that it can be traced to "necessity on specific regressions and hill-climbing performance metrics."

The energy breakdown shows the trade. A Frostbite quad cuts memory energy to 38% and fetch, decode, and issue to 6%. In exchange, it spends 26% on the on-chip network and scheduler. Frostbite moves energy from guessing about dependencies to moving messages between tiles.

What the numbers do not show yet

The baseline is a small core, and it is not named. A dual-issue, in-order core is far simpler than the out-of-order cores in laptops and servers. One HN commenter pointed this out: "Actual modern high-performance CPUs use way larger than dual-issue front-ends." The post says comparisons against larger out-of-order CPUs, multicore setups, and the SPEC and PARSEC benchmark suites are planned "in the coming months".

The power numbers are pre-silicon. They come from models and RTL (hardware description code), not a measured chip. The post says they can be matched to real chips "over multiple tapeout loops", which has not happened yet.

The held-out score is the one to quote. The post reports both 6.02x on tuning workloads and 3.83x on held-out ones. When someone repeats "4.59x", remember that 3.83x is the number for programs the design never saw.

The workloads are small. Three kernels follow the SPLASH-2 suite but are "64 times smaller", per the post. Another HN commenter noted that the tests are compute-heavy kernels on small working sets, and asked how the design handles programs that "build large data structures and slowly mutate them."

Debugging changes. A commenter pointed out that there is no call stack or program counter, and that nets can leak values or get stuck waiting on each other. Vine's own statistics page touches on this: the Allocated and Freed memory numbers should always match, and "if they differ, that indicates that there was a vicious circle in the interaction net." Vine has a debug mode, but the same commenter called a source-level debugger "a requirement" and said that building one, if it does not exist yet, "would represent a substantial engineering project."

Some framing is disputed. The Frostbite post and the Tendrils explainer both say single-core CPU performance has largely stalled since the early 2000s; one commenter disagreed, citing yearly gains in Apple's chips. Another argued that the ideas came from decades of human research, and the AI turned them into an engineered product.

Who builds what

Two companies appear in this story. Architect Labs built Frostbite; its launch post mentions "$24M in seed funding led by Kindred Ventures". Tendrils develops Vine; its November 10 announcement says it raised $30M in a round led by Benchmark to build its own processor "to have thousands of cores operating in parallel."

The Frostbite post cites Vine and the Tendrils explainer. An HN commenter asked whether the two companies are related. Neither post says, so treat them as separate projects that share a language.

The Frostbite post lists its next steps: an FPGA-hosted playground where anyone can run programs, a basic operating system, benchmarks against a broader set of CPUs, and a release of the RTL and ISA.

What you can do with this today

  • Run your algorithms with --breadth-first. Depth and breadth show how much of your code is a serial chain and how much is independent work. If a rewrite lowers depth, it has more room for parallel speedup on any machine.
  • Notice where you share mutable state. Interaction nets make every copy and drop explicit. Asking "who owns this value?" in Java, Go, or Rust is the same habit that makes concurrent code safer.
  • Watch for the FPGA playground and the SPEC results. They will show whether the 3.83x held-out number survives real hardware and stronger baselines.

Frostbite may or may not become a product. The model under it is well defined and available now in a language you can install with one command.

Would you write code for a chip with no program counter and no shared memory, if the tooling caught leaks and stuck nets for you?

Sources

  • [1] Introducing Frostbite, Architect Labs
  • [2] Hacker News discussion of Frostbite
  • [3] On Interaction Nets, Tendrils
  • [4] Interaction nets, Wikipedia (cites Lafont, POPL 1990)
  • [5] Vine documentation
  • [6] Vine on GitHub
  • [7] Vine docs: Fork and Drop
  • [8] Vine docs: Using the CLI
  • [9] Vine docs: Statistics
  • [10] Introducing Architect Labs
  • [11] Tendrils: $30M Raised to Redo the CPU

articles.title: JavaScript Promises, Visualized: The Event Loop Behind Node.js
articles.description: Your Node.js API passes every test. In production, Kubernetes marks a Pod as not ready a few times an...
articles.body_html:
Your Node.js API passes every test. In production, Kubernetes marks a Pod as not ready a few times an hour, and nothing in the logs explains it. No request returned an error, and the CPU is not at its limit. A common cause is one block of synchronous code that holds the only thread your JavaScript runs on. While it runs, the health check request sits unread in a socket, and the probe times out.

To see why, you need a clear picture of how JavaScript runs promises: one call stack, a microtask queue, a task queue, and the event loop that moves callbacks between them. This post builds that picture with small examples, static diagrams and three animations. Then it adds what Node.js does on top, because that is where the production problems come from: process.nextTick, setImmediate, the event loop phases, unhandled rejections, and event loop delay metrics. Every output below comes from running the code with Node.js 24.22.3.

TL;DR

  • JavaScript runs your code on one call stack. Promise callbacks wait in the microtask queue. Timer and I/O callbacks wait in the task queue (in Node.js, in one queue per event loop phase).
  • When the stack is empty, the event loop runs every microtask, then one task, then all microtasks again. That is why a promise callback runs before a 0 ms timer.
  • await splits a function in two. The code before it runs now. The code after it runs later as a microtask, even when the awaited value is ready.
  • In Node.js, the process.nextTick queue drains before promise callbacks, but a nextTick never interrupts a microtask drain that is already running. The top level of an ES module runs inside one, so there promise callbacks go first. Inside an I/O callback, setImmediate always runs before a 0 ms setTimeout.
  • A 2.4 second synchronous report made a /healthz probe with a 1 second timeout fail. The same report in a worker thread left /healthz answering in 7 ms.
  • A rejected promise with no handler stops the process (the default since Node.js 15). Hand related promises to Promise.all so they all have a handler right away.
  • Measure event loop delay with perf_hooks.monitorEventLoopDelay() and performance.eventLoopUtilization(), and alert on the p99 and max.

Prerequisites

  • Node.js 20 or newer. We ran every example with Node.js 24.22.3 and checked the browser-side examples in Chromium 156.
  • Basic JavaScript: functions, arrow functions, and the async and await keywords.
  • For the health check section, a basic idea of Kubernetes readiness and liveness probes. Our Kubernetes Pods guide covers them.

The parts that run your code

Before any promise code, it helps to name the parts. There are five, and only one of them runs JavaScript.

  • Call stack. The JavaScript engine (V8 in Node.js and Chrome) runs one function at a time. When a function calls another, the new one goes on top of the stack. When it returns, it comes off. Your JavaScript never runs two things at once on this thread.
  • The host. Node.js or the browser does the waiting. A timer, a socket read or a file read happens outside the call stack. In Node.js, the libuv library handles this with the operating system and a small thread pool. Your code does not stop while it waits.
  • Microtask queue. Promise callbacks wait here: the functions you pass to then and catch, and the rest of an async function after an await. queueMicrotask() adds to it directly.
  • Task queue. Callbacks from timers and I/O wait here. Browsers call each of these a task. This is a simplified picture: browsers keep several task queues and choose between them, and Node.js keeps one queue per event loop phase, which we look at later.
  • Event loop. The rule that connects them: wait until the stack is empty, run every microtask (including new ones added along the way), then run one task, and repeat.

Keep that rule in mind. Almost every ordering question in this post follows from it.

A promise is a placeholder with a list of callbacks

A promise is an object that stands for a result you do not have yet. It starts pending. Later it settles, once: it becomes fulfilled with a value or rejected with an error. Code that needs the result registers a callback with then, catch or await. When the promise settles, the callbacks for that outcome go into the microtask queue: then callbacks when it is fulfilled, catch callbacks when it is rejected.

Two details of this surprise people. First, the function you pass to new Promise (the executor) runs right away, inside the constructor call. Second, a then callback never runs right away, even when the promise is already fulfilled.

console.log('1. script starts');

const ready = new Promise((resolve) => {
  console.log('2. executor runs right away');
  resolve('config loaded');
});

ready.then((value) => console.log('4. then callback:', value));

console.log('3. script ends');


$ node executor.js
1. script starts
2. executor runs right away
3. script ends
4. then callback: config loaded

The executor printed line 2 before the script reached line 3. The then callback printed last, after the script finished, even though resolve had already been called. Settling a promise only queues its callbacks. They run when the stack is empty.

One detail for later: if you resolve a promise with another promise, it follows that promise instead, so it can still end up rejected. And a promise settles only once. Here the second and third calls do nothing:

const p = new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  resolve('first');
  reject(new Error('ignored'));
  resolve('also ignored');
});
p.then((v) => console.log('value:', v));


$ node settle-once.js
value: first

Watch five lines run

Here is the smallest example that shows the whole rule. Each line logs a letter, and the letters follow the order in which they print, not the order of the lines in the file. The puzzle is why those two orders differ.

console.log('A');
setTimeout(() => console.log('E'), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('C'));
queueMicrotask(() => console.log('D'));
console.log('B');


$ node five-lines.js
A
B
C
D
E

Press play to follow it through the call stack and both queues, one step at a time.

Five lines through the call stack, the microtask queue and the task queue. The script prints A and B, the two microtasks print C and D, and only then does the timer callback print E.

In words:

  1. Lines 1 and 5 run on the call stack and print A and B.
  2. setTimeout(fn, 0) does not run fn. It asks the host for a timer. Zero milliseconds means "as soon as possible", and that can never be before the current script ends. When the timer is due, its callback waits in the task queue.
  3. Promise.resolve() returns a promise that is already fulfilled, so then queues callback C right away. queueMicrotask queues D behind it.
  4. The script ends and the stack is empty. The event loop runs every microtask first: C, then D.
  5. Only then does it take the next task, the timer callback, which prints E.

We ran the same five lines in Chromium 156 and got the same A B C D E. Browsers and Node.js agree on this part. If you want to step through more cases like this, including rejections and Promise.all, try the JavaScript Promises and Async/Await Simulator.

async and await use the same queues

An async function always returns a promise. Inside it, await takes a promise (or any value) and pauses the function until that promise settles. The pause does not block the thread. At the first await, the function returns its pending promise to the caller, and the rest of its body runs later as a microtask.

const getUser = async () => ({ id: 42 }); // already cached, so it resolves at once

async function handleRequest() {
  console.log('2. before');
  const user = await getUser();
  console.log('4. after', user.id);
}

console.log('1. script starts');
handleRequest(); // returns a pending promise here
console.log('3. script ends');


$ node await-split.js
1. script starts
2. before
3. script ends
4. after 42

Read the output as two halves. Line 2 printed before the call returned, so the first half of handleRequest ran as part of the caller. Line 4 printed after the script ended, even though getUser had nothing to wait for. An await always pauses, even for a value that is ready: the rest of the function runs only after the code that is running now has finished.

The same mechanism lets functions take turns. Here two calls are started up front, and they interleave at each await:

async function request(name) {
  console.log(`${name}: parse body`);
  await null; // pretend this is a database call that is already cached
  console.log(`${name}: query done`);
  await null;
  console.log(`${name}: send response`);
}

request('req-1');
request('req-2');
console.log('main: both requests started');


$ node interleave.js
req-1: parse body
req-2: parse body
main: both requests started
req-1: query done
req-2: query done
req-1: send response
req-2: send response

Two calls, one thread, and the work takes turns at every await. None of your JavaScript runs in parallel. With await null the turns happen inside one pass over the microtask queue. In a real server, an await on real I/O, such as a database query, also hands the thread back to the event loop, and that is when a new request can start. That is fine while each turn is short. The rest of this post is about what happens when a turn is long, or when Node.js schedules work in a way you did not expect.

What Node.js adds: nextTick, setImmediate and phases

Everything so far works the same in browsers and Node.js. Node.js adds two scheduling functions, process.nextTick() and setImmediate(), which browsers do not have (in Chromium 156, typeof setImmediate and typeof process both return 'undefined'). It also splits its task queue into phases.

The Node.js event loop phases

  1. timers setTimeout, setInterval
  2. pending deferred system callbacks
  3. poll I/O: sockets, files
  4. check setImmediate
  5. close close events

back to timers, then back to step 1.

Each phase has its own callback queue. The timers phase runs due setTimeout and setInterval callbacks. Poll runs most I/O callbacks, such as socket data and finished file reads, and waits for new I/O when there is nothing else to do. Check runs setImmediate callbacks. Close runs handlers such as socket.on('close'). The pending phase runs a few deferred system callbacks, and you rarely need to think about it.

Between callbacks, Node.js drains two queues: first the process.nextTick queue, then the promise microtask queue, and it repeats until both are empty. This happens after every callback the event loop runs (a timer, an I/O callback, a setImmediate), not once per phase:

for (const n of [1, 2]) {
  setTimeout(() => {
    console.log(`timer ${n}`);
    process.nextTick(() => console.log(` nextTick from timer ${n}`));
    Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log(` promise from timer ${n}`));
  }, 0);
}


$ node between-callbacks.js
timer 1
  nextTick from timer 1
  promise from timer 1
timer 2
  nextTick from timer 2
  promise from timer 2

Now put all four scheduling calls in one file:

setTimeout(() => console.log('setTimeout 0'), 0);
setImmediate(() => console.log('setImmediate'));
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('promise then'));
process.nextTick(() => console.log('process.nextTick'));
console.log('sync code');

Run it as a CommonJS file and as an ES module, and the first two callbacks swap places:

$ node order.js
sync code
process.nextTick
promise then
setTimeout 0
setImmediate

$ cp order.js order.mjs && node order.mjs
sync code
promise then
process.nextTick
setTimeout 0
setImmediate

The reason is how Node.js starts an ES module. It loads ES modules with async code, so your top-level code runs while V8 is already working through the microtask queue. A promise callback you queue there runs in that same pass, before Node.js gets back to its nextTick queue. In a CommonJS file there is no such pass, so nextTick goes first. The same rule applies inside any promise callback: a nextTick queued there waits until the microtask queue is empty.

Promise.resolve().then(() => {
  process.nextTick(() => console.log('nextTick queued inside a promise callback'));
  Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('promise queued inside a promise callback'));
});


$ node tick-inside-microtask.js
promise queued inside a promise callback
nextTick queued inside a promise callback

The safe lesson: do not write code that depends on nextTick versus promise order.

The last two lines of the order.js output need a warning too. On our machine, setTimeout 0 came before setImmediate in 200 of 200 runs of both files. The Node.js event loop docs say this order is not guaranteed in the main module, because it depends on how fast the process reaches the loop. Inside an I/O callback, the order is fixed. Press play to watch one turn of the loop:

A readFile callback runs in the poll phase and schedules four callbacks. The nextTick queue drains first, then promise microtasks, then the check phase runs setImmediate, and the timer waits until the loop wraps around to timers.

const fs = require('node:fs');
const log = (msg) => console.log(msg);

fs.readFile(__filename, () => {
  setTimeout(() => log('timeout'), 0);
  setImmediate(() => log('immediate'));
  Promise.resolve().then(() => log('promise'));
  process.nextTick(() => log('nextTick'));
  log('readFile callback');
});


$ node io-order.js
readFile callback
nextTick
promise
immediate
timeout

We ran it 200 times and immediate came before timeout every time. The check phase comes right after poll, so a setImmediate queued during an I/O callback always runs before the loop gets back to timers. Use setImmediate when you want to run something after the current I/O work, and setTimeout(fn, 0) only when you mean a timer.

These rules are for Node.js. Other runtimes, such as Bun, implement their own event loop, so check the Bun vs Node.js comparison and test on your runtime before you rely on fine-grained ordering. We only tested Node.js here.

A busy event loop fails health checks

Now the production problem from the start of this post. Here is a small HTTP server with two routes. /healthz answers at once. /report builds a CSV report in memory: it creates 300,000 rows, sorts them and joins them into a string. All of that is synchronous JavaScript.

// report.js
function buildReport(rowCount) {
  const rows = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < rowCount; i++) {
    rows.push({ id: i, customer: `cust-${(i * 7919) % rowCount}`, total: (i * 37) % 1000 });
  }
  rows.sort((a, b) => a.customer.localeCompare(b.customer));
  return rows.map((r) => `${r.id},${r.customer},${r.total}`).join('\n');
}
module.exports = { buildReport };


// server.js
const http = require('node:http');
const path = require('node:path');
const { Worker } = require('node:worker_threads');
const { buildReport } = require('./report');

const MODE = process.env.MODE || 'sync'; // sync | worker
const ROWS = Number(process.env.ROWS || 300000);

function reportInWorker(rows) {
  return new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
    const worker = new Worker(path.join(__dirname, 'report-worker.js'), { workerData: { rows } });
    worker.once('message', resolve);
    worker.once('error', reject);
  });
}

http
  .createServer(async (req, res) => {
    if (req.url === '/healthz') return res.end('ok\n');
    if (req.url === '/report') {
      const t0 = performance.now();
      const bytes = MODE === 'worker' ? await reportInWorker(ROWS) : buildReport(ROWS).length;
      const ms = Math.round(performance.now() - t0);
      return res.end(`report ${bytes} bytes in ${ms} ms (${MODE})\n`);
    }
    res.statusCode = 404;
    res.end();
  })
  .listen(8080, () => console.log(`listening on :8080, mode=${MODE}`));


// report-worker.js
const { parentPort, workerData } = require('node:worker_threads');
const { buildReport } = require('./report');

parentPort.postMessage(buildReport(workerData.rows).length);

To keep the demo short, the handler has no error path. In a real service, wrap the await in try/catch and answer with a 500, because a crashed worker would otherwise become an unhandled rejection, and the next sections show why that is fatal.

The client below acts like a kubelet probe with a 1 second timeout. It checks /healthz once while the server is idle, then starts a report and sends a second /healthz 100 ms later:

// probe.js
const base = 'http://127.0.0.1:8080';

async function timed(path, timeoutMs) {
  const t0 = performance.now();
  try {
    const res = await fetch(base + path, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(timeoutMs) });
    const body = (await res.text()).trim();
    return `${path} -> ${res.status} in ${Math.round(performance.now() - t0)} ms (${body})`;
  } catch (err) {
    return `${path} -> FAILED after ${Math.round(performance.now() - t0)} ms (${err.name})`;
  }
}

(async () => {
  await timed('/healthz', 1000); // warm-up: the first fetch loads its HTTP client
  console.log('idle: ' + (await timed('/healthz', 1000)));
  const report = timed('/report', 30000);
  await new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, 100)); // probe arrives 100 ms later
  console.log('busy: ' + (await timed('/healthz', 1000)));
  console.log('the work: ' + (await report));
})();

With the report on the main thread:

$ MODE=sync node server.js &
listening on :8080, mode=sync
$ node probe.js
idle: /healthz -> 200 in 13 ms (ok)
busy: /healthz -> FAILED after 1008 ms (TimeoutError)
the work: /report -> 200 in 2450 ms (report 6644779 bytes in 2437 ms (sync))
$ kill %1

With the same report in a worker thread:

$ MODE=worker node server.js &
listening on :8080, mode=worker
$ node probe.js
idle: /healthz -> 200 in 15 ms (ok)
busy: /healthz -> 200 in 7 ms (ok)
the work: /report -> 200 in 2257 ms (report 6644779 bytes in 2241 ms (worker))
$ kill %1

We ran each mode five times. The synchronous report took 2.3 to 2.5 seconds, and the probe failed in every run. With the worker, the probe that arrived during the report got its answer in 7 to 19 ms. The worker times include starting the worker and sending the result back.

The two measured runs above as a timeline. On the main thread, the report holds the event loop for 2.4 seconds and the probe gives up after 1 second. In a worker thread, the same report takes 2.2 seconds and /healthz answers in 7 ms.

The /healthz handler is one line, but it is a callback like any other. It can only run when the call stack is empty, and the report kept the stack busy for 2.4 seconds. The kernel completed the TCP connection, but Node.js could not accept it or read the request until the report was done. By then the probe had given up.

On Kubernetes, a probe has timeoutSeconds: 1, periodSeconds: 10 and failureThreshold: 3 unless you set them. One slow answer is one failure. Three failures in a row on a readiness probe mark the Pod as not ready, so Services stop sending it traffic. Three in a row on a liveness probe make the kubelet restart the container, which can cut off requests that are still in flight. One report is not enough for that, but a burst of report requests, or a batch job that keeps the loop busy for half a minute, is. That is how a Pod ends up flapping between ready and not ready with no error in its logs.

Raising timeoutSeconds hides the symptom, but every user request on that Pod still waits behind the report. Fix the cause instead:

  1. Move CPU-heavy work off the event loop. Use worker_threads, a job queue with a separate worker process, or a separate service. Sorting, compressing, hashing with the *Sync APIs and parsing very large JSON are common examples. The demo above starts one worker per request to keep the code short. In production, use a small, fixed-size worker pool with a bounded queue, or a burst of reports will use up CPU and memory and slow the probes again.
  2. Break long loops into chunks. Yield to the event loop between chunks, as shown in the next section.
  3. Keep probes cheap and honest. A liveness probe should only check that the process can answer. Load-test the Pod with the probe running, not only the endpoints.

Microtask floods block the loop too

You might think async code cannot block, because it is full of await. It can. An await on a value that is already available still queues a microtask, and the event loop keeps running microtasks until the queue is empty. Timers and I/O wait the whole time.

const { setImmediate: yieldToLoop } = require('node:timers/promises');

const skus = Array.from({ length: 2_000_000 }, (_, i) => `sku-${i % 1000}`);
const prices = new Map(Array.from({ length: 1000 }, (_, i) => [`sku-${i}`, i]));

// Looks async, but the price is already in memory, so each
// await resolves at once and only queues another microtask.
async function getPrice(sku) {
  return prices.get(sku);
}

async function priceAll(label, yieldEvery) {
  const t0 = performance.now();
  setTimeout(() => {
    console.log(`${label}: 0 ms timer ran after ${Math.round(performance.now() - t0)} ms`);
  }, 0);
  let total = 0;
  for (let i = 0; i < skus.length; i++) {
    total += await getPrice(skus[i]);
    if (yieldEvery && (i + 1) % yieldEvery === 0) await yieldToLoop(); // let timers and I/O run
  }
  console.log(`${label}: priced ${skus.length} items in ${Math.round(performance.now() - t0)} ms`);
}

(async () => {
  await priceAll('no yield', 0);
  await priceAll('yield every 10000', 10_000);
})();


$ node microtask-flood.js
no yield: priced 2000000 items in 1436 ms
no yield: 0 ms timer ran after 1455 ms
yield every 10000: 0 ms timer ran after 8 ms
yield every 10000: priced 2000000 items in 1324 ms

When did a 0 ms timer get to run?

Value Series
no yield 1455ms Await only
yield every 10,000 items 8ms Await plus setImmediate

microtask-flood.js on Node.js 24.22.3. The job awaits 2,000,000 values that are already in memory. Yielding with setImmediate every 10,000 items gave the timer a turn after 8 ms.

Without a yield, the timer waited for the whole job. With await setImmediate() every 10,000 items, the loop got a turn every few milliseconds, and the job did not get slower. setImmediate works here because it is not a microtask. Awaiting it hands control back to the event loop, and the function only continues in the check phase, so timers and I/O callbacks that are due get their turn in between.

Recursive process.nextTick calls do the same thing, because the nextTick queue also drains completely before the loop moves on. In our run, 3,000,000 recursive ticks delayed a 0 ms timer by 1,415 ms.

Unhandled rejections stop the process

Since Node.js 15, the default for --unhandled-rejections is throw. If a rejected promise has no handler and you do not listen for the unhandledRejection event, Node.js raises it like an uncaught exception, and the process exits with code 1. Before that, Node.js printed a warning and kept going, and a lot of older advice still assumes that.

async function refreshToken() {
  throw new Error('token endpoint returned 503');
}

setInterval(() => console.log('still serving requests'), 200);

refreshToken(); // nobody awaits it and nobody calls .catch()
console.log('refresh started');


$ node unhandled.js; echo "exit code: $?"
refresh started
unhandled.js:2
  throw new Error('token endpoint returned 503');
        ^

Error: token endpoint returned 503
    at refreshToken (unhandled.js:2:9)
    ...

Node.js v24.22.3
exit code: 1

We shortened the stack trace. The interval never printed once: the process exited at the end of the first turn, as soon as Node.js saw a rejected promise with no handler.

The harder version of this bug has a handler, but attaches it too late. Here both requests start together, and the function awaits them one after the other:

const wait = (ms, fail) =>
  new Promise((resolve, reject) =>
    setTimeout(() => (fail ? reject(new Error(`${fail} failed`)) : resolve(ms)), ms)
  );

async function loadDashboard() {
  const user = wait(300); // slow, succeeds
  const invoices = wait(50, 'invoices'); // fast, fails
  try {
    console.log('user', await user); // still waiting here at 50 ms...
    console.log('invoices', await invoices); // ...so this handler is attached too late
  } catch (err) {
    console.log('caught:', err.message);
  }
}

loadDashboard();


$ node late-handler.js; echo "exit code: $?"
late-handler.js:3
    setTimeout(() => (fail ? reject(new Error(`${fail} failed`)) : resolve(ms)), ms)
                                    ^

Error: invoices failed
    at Timeout._onTimeout (late-handler.js:3:37)
    ...

Node.js v24.22.3
exit code: 1

The try and catch look correct, but at 50 ms the function is still waiting on user. Nothing has called then or await on invoices yet, so its rejection has no handler, and Node.js exits. The fix is to hand both promises to Promise.all, which attaches a handler to each of them right away. wait() is the same helper as above:

async function loadDashboard() {
  try {
    // Promise.all attaches a handler to both promises right away.
    const [user, invoices] = await Promise.all([wait(300), wait(50, 'invoices')]);
    console.log('user', user, 'invoices', invoices);
  } catch (err) {
    console.log('caught:', err.message);
  }
}


$ node late-handler-fixed.js; echo "exit code: $?"
caught: invoices failed
exit code: 0

Use Promise.allSettled instead when you want every result, including the failed ones.

For the rejections you did not plan for, keep the default mode and add a process-level hook that logs with context and then exits on purpose:

const fs = require('node:fs');

process.on('unhandledRejection', (reason) => {
  // Log it with context, then exit so the orchestrator restarts a clean process.
  // writeSync: on a pipe, stderr is asynchronous and process.exit() does not wait for it.
  const line = JSON.stringify({
    level: 'fatal',
    event: 'unhandledRejection',
    error: String(reason),
  });
  fs.writeSync(2, line + '\n');
  process.exit(1);
});

We put that hook at the top of a file that calls the failing refreshToken() from above:

$ node unhandled-hook.js; echo "exit code: $?"
{"level":"fatal","event":"unhandledRejection","error":"Error: token endpoint returned 503"}
exit code: 1

Do not switch to --unhandled-rejections=warn to make crashes go away. We tried it on unhandled.js: the process printed a warning and kept serving, with a failed token refresh that nothing will ever retry. A restart from a clean state is usually the safer failure.

Measure event loop delay

You cannot fix event loop blocking that you cannot see. Node.js has two built-in measurements in perf_hooks:

  • monitorEventLoopDelay() starts a timer that should fire every resolution milliseconds and records the time between firings, as a histogram in nanoseconds. When the loop is blocked, the timer fires late and the gap grows.
  • performance.eventLoopUtilization() reports the share of time the event loop was busy, running callbacks or stuck in synchronous code, instead of idle and waiting for I/O.

This script measures 2 idle seconds, then 2 seconds that contain three 250 ms synchronous steps:

const { monitorEventLoopDelay, performance } = require('node:perf_hooks');

const h = monitorEventLoopDelay({ resolution: 10 }); // sample every 10 ms
h.enable();
let lastElu = performance.eventLoopUtilization();

function report(label) {
  const elu = performance.eventLoopUtilization(lastElu); // delta since last report
  lastElu = performance.eventLoopUtilization();
  const ms = (ns) => (ns / 1e6).toFixed(1);
  console.log(
    `${label.padEnd(16)} delay p50=${ms(h.percentile(50))}ms p99=${ms(h.percentile(99))}ms` +
      ` max=${ms(h.max)}ms utilization=${(elu.utilization * 100).toFixed(0)}%`
  );
  h.reset();
}

// A stand-in for synchronous work: spin for `ms` milliseconds.
function busy(ms) {
  const end = Date.now() + ms;
  while (Date.now() < end);
}

setTimeout(() => report('idle 2 s'), 2000);
setTimeout(() => {
  for (const at of [500, 1000, 1500]) setTimeout(() => busy(250), at); // three 250 ms sync steps
  setTimeout(() => {
    report('busy 2 s');
    h.disable();
  }, 2000);
}, 2000);


$ node loop-delay.js
idle 2 s delay p50=10.1ms p99=12.9ms max=13.9ms utilization=0%
busy 2 s delay p50=10.1ms p99=256.6ms max=257.2ms utilization=38%

Two details make these numbers easier to read. First, the values include the sampling interval: with resolution: 10, an idle loop shows about 10 ms, so the real extra delay is the value minus 10. Second, the 38% utilization matches the three steps: 750 ms of busy time in a 2,000 ms window. The p99 and max show the 250 ms stalls, while p50 stayed at 10.1 ms. That is why you alert on the p99 or max, not on the median. Keep an eye on request latency too: a rare long stall can hide below the p99 but still show up in the max.

In production you do not need to write this yourself. If you already use prom-client, collectDefaultMetrics() uses monitorEventLoopDelay and exports gauges such as nodejs_eventloop_lag_p99_seconds. A useful alert is a p99 that stays above a threshold you choose well below your probe timeout, for example a few hundred milliseconds when timeoutSeconds is 1. When it fires, take a CPU profile (node --cpu-prof) during a busy period to find the synchronous code that holds the loop.

A checklist for Node.js services

  • Keep every synchronous step short. Move CPU-bound work to worker_threads, a job queue or another service.
  • In long loops, yield with await setImmediate() from node:timers/promises every few thousand items. Many awaits on ready values do not yield.
  • Do not depend on process.nextTick versus promise order, or on setTimeout(fn, 0) versus setImmediate in top-level code. The first flipped between CommonJS and ES modules in our tests, and the Node.js docs say the second is not guaranteed.
  • Start related promises together and hand them to Promise.all or Promise.allSettled, so each one has a handler from the start.
  • Keep the default unhandled rejection mode. Add an unhandledRejection hook that logs with context and exits.
  • Export event loop delay p99 and utilization, and alert well below your probe timeout.
  • Load-test with probes enabled, and treat probe failures under load as a code problem before you change the timeouts.

If you want to check your understanding, the APIs, async and config quiz has a microtask ordering question, and the concurrency and race conditions quiz asks what happens when a request blocks the event loop.

Further reading

  • Lydia Hallie, JavaScript Visualized: Promise Execution (archived copy). A great visual explainer of what happens inside a promise, with animations of each step.
  • Node.js docs: The Node.js Event Loop, Understanding process.nextTick(), perf_hooks and the --unhandled-rejections flag.
  • MDN: Using microtasks in JavaScript with queueMicrotask().
  • Kubernetes: Liveness, Readiness, and Startup Probes.

Still reaching for Redux every time you need to manage state in a React application?

There's a simpler approach worth learning: Zustand.

Zustand is a lightweight state management library for React that makes it easy to share and update state without a lot of boilerplate. And if you'd like to learn it hands-on, I'm making my popular Getting Started with Zustand course available with lifetime FREE access 🎉

Why Learn Zustand?

As React applications grow, managing shared state across components can become challenging. Zustand offers a straightforward way to create stores, access state, update it, and organize state management logic.

In this practical course, you'll learn the fundamentals and apply them to real applications—not just isolated examples.

📚 What You'll Learn

🧠 Zustand fundamentals: Stores, selectors, middleware, DevTools and asynchronous actions.
🌐 API integration: Manage state while working with API calls and asynchronous data.
🔄 Immutable state updates: Update objects, arrays and nested state; learn how Immer can help.
🧰 Custom hooks and debugging: Organize and troubleshoot your state management code.
