articles.title: Stateful Observable: loading, errors and combined data in RxJS without the boilerplate
articles.description: Why I stopped writing tap(() => this.loading = true).  Every Angular codebase I have worked on has...
articles.body_html:
Why I stopped writing tap(() => this.loading = true).

Every Angular codebase I have worked on has the same few lines somewhere, usually in many places: a loading flag set from a tap, an error field set from a catchError, and a shareReplay somewhere in between.

It works for the happy path. Then someone adds a second async pipe to the template and the request goes out twice. A failure path forgets to reset loading, and the spinner never goes away. Someone combines this stream with another one, and now there are two loading flags and two error fields to merge by hand. A user logs out, and a shareReplay(1) three services away still replays the previous user's data.

When I searched GitHub for tap(() => this.loading, I got about 12 thousand files. That number has no denominator, but it does show that this pattern is everywhere.

This article is about Stateful Observable (@rx-evo/stateful-observable on npm), a small library I built on top of RxJS to replace that boilerplate. A stateful observable is an observable that carries its own loading, error and inactive state, survives errors, shares itself by default and combines with other stateful observables. On top of that it gives you a dataflow graph that you can recover from any node.

npm install @rx-evo/stateful-observable

The library depends only on RxJS. My examples are written for Angular because that is where the library started, but it isn't tied to Angular. It runs in Node.js too, more on that below.

It looks like a small thing. It isn't.

One tap for a loading flag or one shareReplay doesn't look like much. The trouble is that they don't come alone. Here is the data part of a component based on a real one from my demo app. It shows a client and the client's bucket enriched with a product catalog:

export class StreamComponent {
  public readonly clientId = input.required<number>();
  private readonly clientId$ = toObservable(this.clientId);

  public readonly clientLoading$ = new BehaviorSubject(true);
  public readonly bucketLoading$ = new BehaviorSubject(true);
  public readonly productsLoading$ = new BehaviorSubject(true);

  public readonly client$ = this.clientId$.pipe(
    tap(() => this.clientLoading$.next(true)),
    switchMap((clientId) => this.clientsApi.getClient$(clientId)),
    tap(() => this.clientLoading$.next(false)),
  );
  private readonly bucket$ = this.clientId$.pipe(
    tap(() => this.bucketLoading$.next(true)),
    switchMap((clientId) => this.bucketApi.getClientBucket$(clientId)),
    tap(() => this.bucketLoading$.next(false)),
  );
  private readonly products$ = this.productsApi
    .allProducts$()
    .pipe(tap(() => this.productsLoading$.next(false)));

  public readonly populatedBucket$ = combineLatest([
    this.bucket$,
    this.products$,
  ]).pipe(
    map(([bucket, products]) => prepareBucket(bucket, products)),
    shareReplay(1),
  );

  public readonly combinedLoading$ = combineLatest([
    this.bucketLoading$,
    this.productsLoading$,
  ]).pipe(map((arr) => arr.some(Boolean)));
}

The business logic here is three API calls and one prepareBucket. Everything else is plumbing: three mutable loading subjects, five taps that write to them, a hand-merged combinedLoading$, and a shareReplay on one stream but not on the others. Each of those is a decision someone had to get right.

And this version has no error handling at all. If the bucket request fails, bucket$ ends, populatedBucket$ ends with it, bucketLoading$ stays true, and the spinner spins forever. A new clientId doesn't help, because the stream is already dead. Adding error handling means a catchError and an error subject per stream, and one more hand-merged combinedError$. The noise roughly doubles.

The same component with Stateful Observable:

private readonly clientId$ = statefulObservable(toObservable(this.clientId));
private readonly allProducts$ = inject(allProductsToken); // shared, app-wide

public readonly client$ = this.clientId$.pipeValue(
  switchMap((id) => this.clientsApi.getClient$(id)),
);
private readonly bucket$ = this.clientId$.pipeValue(
  switchMap((id) => this.bucketApi.getClientBucket$(id)),
);

public readonly populatedBucket$ = combineStatefulObservables(
  [this.bucket$, this.allProducts$],
  ([bucket, products]) => prepareBucket(bucket, products),
);

What's left is the business logic. Loading, errors, recovery after a failure and sharing are all there, and you can read each of them from any node: populatedBucket$.pending$, populatedBucket$.error$, populatedBucket$.reload().

What I wanted to fix

I started with a list of problems I kept running into on real projects:

  1. Common RxJS misuses that cost requests. The best-known one is a missing shareReplay, which turns every extra subscriber into another HTTP request.
  2. Loading flags set by hand. No more tap(() => this.loading.set(true)).
  3. Errors that end the stream. I wanted error handling and recovery built in, not written by hand for each stream.
  4. Combining several data sources, each with its own loading and error state, in a way that behaves correctly.
  5. A dataflow graph that costs nothing to build. Once 1–4 are solved, that graph is what you get.

I'll go through them in that order.

1. Shared by default: no accidental extra requests

A plain observable is cold. Every subscription runs the whole pipeline again. If you bind one stream in a template three times (value, pending flag, error), you send three requests. In a measured run with a hand-written state operator, three subscriptions made three requests, and adding shareReplay brought it down to one.

Adding shareReplay is easy to forget. Once you remember it, you have more choices to make: refCount or not, and how to reset the buffer later (shareReplay has no reset, which matters at logout).

A stateful observable is shared by default. Each node caches its raw stream with shareReplay({ bufferSize: 1, refCount: true }), so all subscribers share one request and the source is released when the last one leaves:

import { statefulObservable } from "@rx-evo/stateful-observable";

const client$ = statefulObservable({
  input: clientId$,
  loader: (id: number) => api.getClient(id),
});

// value$, pending$ and error$ together: one request

Data that should live for the whole app is one option away:

const products$ = statefulObservable({
  loader: () => api.allProducts(),
  refCount: false, // keep it without subscribers
});

It is still lazy. Nothing happens until something subscribes, so a section rendered under @if starts its request when it is expanded and releases it when it collapses. You don't write any code for that.

2. Loading state without tap

A stateful observable exposes three derived streams next to the values:

  • value$: successful values only
  • pending$: true while a change was started and has no result yet
  • error$: errors, as values

All three are derived from one cached raw$ stream, so they always agree with each other. Nothing in your code writes to them. Loading is derived from the loader, not set from a tap. In a template, using the client$ from the component above:

<div [class.loading]="client$.pending$ | async">
  @if (client$.error$ | async; as error) {
    <app-error [error]="error" (retry)="client$.reload()" />
  } @else {
    <app-client [client]="client$.value$ | async" />
  }
</div>

Two details took me several attempts to get right:

The previous value stays on screen while new data loads. A new pending event does not clear the last value. Only a new value or a new error replaces it. Many "wrap the response" helpers emit { loading: true, value: null } on every request, which wipes the content and makes the layout jump. I didn't want that.

Loading is emitted only for work that is actually asynchronous. A cache hit or a synchronous result arrives without a loading event, so pending$ doesn't flicker.

pipeValue and pipeError take ordinary RxJS operators. You don't need special operators that know about wrapped values or if (isLoading(x)) return x branches. switchMap switches, mergeMap runs everything in parallel, and scan and distinctUntilChanged keep their state as they do in plain RxJS.

Why three pipes instead of one

A single pipe over wrapped events would make every operator deal with the state:

// one pipe for everything
source.pipe(
  mergeMap((event) => {
    if (isLoading(event)) return of(event); // bypass
    if (isError(event)) return of(event);   // bypass
    return api.fetchBy(event);
  }),
);
// and concatMap in that place behaves incorrectly

The other way out is a set of helper operators (onlyValue(...) and friends). That's one more API to learn, and it fits badly with operators that weren't written for it. Separate pipes keep ordinary operators working, including higher-order ones:

statefulObservable(formValue$)
  .pipeValue(switchMap((v) => api.fetchBy(v)))  // values only
  .pipeError(map(toTypedError))                 // errors only
  .pipe(takeUntilDestroyed());                  // the whole stream

Plain pipe is for operators that apply to the whole stream: takeUntilDestroyed, shareReplay, debounceTime. And because takeUntilDestroyed goes in through pipe, the library doesn't need Angular to clean up after itself. The full reasoning is in the ADR.

3. Errors are data, and the stream survives them

In RxJS an error ends the stream. In a combineLatest, one failing branch ends the combined stream and everything below it. Recovering takes catchError in the right place, at every level.

In a stateful observable, an error is one of the states. An error thrown in any pipe is caught at that node and sent on as an error event, and the stream goes on to handle the next input:

const result$ = statefulObservable(query$).pipeValue(
  switchMap((q) => this.api.search(q)), // fails for one query...
);
// ...and still delivers the result for the next one

Errors can be typed. You narrow them once at the source, and the type carries through later pipes and combinations:

const products$ = statefulObservable({
  loader: () => api.allProducts(),
  name: "allProducts",
}).pipeError(map(toProductsError)); // error$ is now Observable<ProductsError>

Every node has reload(), so a retry button needs no extra Subject:

<button (click)="client$.reload()">Retry</button>

Errors are also hard to lose. If nothing subscribes to error$, the failure is logged to the console with the node's name and its position in the chain (Unhandled error in statefulObservable 'clientStream #1'). When you subscribe, the message goes away. A stateful observable doesn't swallow errors without a trace.

4. Combining data sources properly

This is the part that tends to go wrong. A bucket enriched with a product catalog looks like this in plain RxJS:

const populatedBucket$ = combineLatest([bucket$, products$]).pipe(
  map(([bucket, products]) => prepareBucket(bucket, products)),
);

That's fine until you need a spinner and an error view. Then you need a rule: is the combination pending if any source is pending? Which error wins? Which source failed? Each team writes this rule a bit differently in each combination.

With combineStatefulObservables the rule is part of the library:

import { combineStatefulObservables } from "@rx-evo/stateful-observable";

const populatedBucket$ = combineStatefulObservables(
  [bucket$, products$],
  ([bucket, products]) => prepareBucket(bucket, products),
);
  • Values come in as a typed tuple ([Bucket, Product[]]), inferred from the sources.
  • The error is a tuple too, with one entry per source: [BucketError | false, ProductsError | false]. You can see exactly which source failed.
  • The priority is the same at every combination: inactive, then pending, then error, then value.
  • An error is emitted only once every source has settled. An error event therefore describes the full state. It is never partial and never extended later, so "retry what failed" reaches everything that failed.
  • While a source is pending, the combination emits pending instead of combining that source's old value with another source's new one. With asynchronous sources this removes the outdated combinations that plain combineLatest briefly emits.

The cost of that rule: an error waits for the slowest source in the same combination. The reasoning and the alternatives I considered are in the ADR.

Combinations nest, and a combined node is a stateful observable like any other. You can pipe it, combine it again and reload it.

Chained requests: where plain RxJS gets tricky

A very common case: load an entity by id, then load a related entity by its foreign key, and show both together.

const entity$ = id$.pipe(
  switchMap((id) => api.fetchEntity(id)),
  shareReplay(1),
);
const relatedEntity$ = entity$.pipe(
  switchMap(({ foreignKey }) => api.fetchRelatedEntity(foreignKey)),
);
const combined$ = combineLatest([entity$, relatedEntity$]);

This is where loading tracking and stale data get difficult:

  • Stale mix. When the id changes, entity$ gets the new entity first, while relatedEntity$ still holds the related entity of the old one. combineLatest emits that pair: the new entity with the old related data, a combination that never existed. In a quick run with two delayed requests and the id going from 1 to 2, the vanilla version emitted 1/10, then 2/10, then 2/20.
  • Loading. The related entity is out of date as soon as the id changes, not when the new entity arrives. So a hand-written relatedLoading flag has to start on the id, not on its own input. Get that wrong, and the old related data is shown as current while the new entity loads.
  • Errors. If either request fails, the whole chain ends, as in the component at the start of this article.

The same with Stateful Observable:

const id$ = statefulObservable(form.valueChanges);

const entity$ = id$.pipeValue(
  switchMap((id) => api.fetchEntity(id)),
);
const relatedEntity$ = entity$.pipeValue(
  switchMap(({ foreignKey }) => api.fetchRelatedEntity(foreignKey)),
);

const combined$ = combineStatefulObservables(
  [entity$, relatedEntity$],
  ([entity, related]) => ({ entity, related }),
);

Pending travels down the chain, so relatedEntity$ is pending as soon as entity$ is, and the combination emits pending instead of pairing new data with old. In the same run, this version emitted 1/10, then pending, then 2/20. The mix was never emitted. Each step has its own pending$ and error$, a failure in the second request leaves the first one on screen, and combined$.reload() reloads the chain.

Split, chain, combine

The library is built for the shapes real dataflows take. A stream gets split into several branches. A branch chains requests, each one depending on the previous. Branches get combined again, either from separate roots (a client's bucket with the app-wide catalog) or by recombining a stream with something derived from it (an entity with its related entity). Each of those shapes has its own edge cases: stale mixes, loading that starts at the wrong moment, errors that end everything. In a stateful observable they're handled the same way at every node. So a reliable dataflow graph takes no extra effort.

In most apps I've seen, this graph is never built. Handling it properly means a lot of boilerplate and edge cases, so the usual shortcut is to merge everything together: one forkJoin, one big request, one store update, one spinner for the whole page. It works, but the cost is real. Nothing renders until the slowest request answers, so there's no progressive loading. One failed endpoint takes down the whole page, so there's no graceful degradation. And the error handling is a single "something went wrong" with no way to retry only the part that failed.

5. The result: a dataflow graph you get for free

Go back to the stateful version of the component at the start of this article. The root token behind allProducts$ is one more declaration:

export const allProductsToken = new InjectionToken("allProducts", {
  providedIn: "root",
  factory: () => {
    const api = inject(ProductsApiService);
    return statefulObservable({
      loader: () => api.allProducts$(),
      name: "allProducts",
      refCount: false, // app-wide data: keep it without subscribers
    });
  },
});

Put together, the pieces form a graph:

Every node has the same handle: value$, pending$, error$, reload(). That brings a few things with it:

Graceful degradation follows from the shape of the graph. Each piece of UI is a leaf that depends only on the sources it needs. A failure blocks only the nodes that depend on it, and every other leaf still renders. If the catalog endpoint is down, the client header still shows.

Progressive rendering is the default. Streams are lazy and each region subscribes to its own sources, so each region renders as soon as those sources answer, without waiting for the rest of the page.

Recovery works from any handle. A template often holds only the final node. reload() on that node reloads every source behind it, through every layer of pipes and combinations. If you add a source to the combination later, the retry button doesn't need to change. You can narrow it down:

populatedBucket$.reload();                                    // everything behind it
populatedBucket$.reload({ onlyFailed: true });                // only what failed
populatedBucket$.reload({ where: ({ name }) => name === "allProducts" }); // by name or meta
populatedBucket$.reload({ path: [1] });                       // by position, as in the error tuple

You don't need a global registry or query keys, and the caller doesn't need to know what the sources are.

The dataflow can be read straight from the code. Derived nodes have no write API, so a value has exactly one producer, and you find where it comes from by following references. The diagram above is redrawn from what angular-mermaider produced for the component. It's a static analyser I wrote as a proof of concept, and it draws this graph without running the app. That only works because the graph is pure.

None of this needs plumbing per layer. In plain RxJS you can build the same thing, but you build it yourself: { data$, reload } pairs from every layer, a combining helper with a rule, a reload method that knows every source. A stateful observable gives every node all of that.

On top of the core, the library has a few tools for real-app problems: active to drop user data at logout, a result cache per input, and factories for lookups by id, with batching. Part 2 shows them at work on a complex page. The quality-of-life guide describes them in detail.

Why not signals, resources or a store?

I tried signals first. Signals are synchronous by nature, which makes laziness hard. In my experiments the requests kept running after the UI that needed them was hidden. By default, Angular's resource resets its value when a new request starts, so large content jumps; keeping it takes a documented extra pattern. Combining several resources needs your own helper, and that helper again has to decide which status wins and which source failed. My notes from those attempts are in the ADR. Signals do work well as the presentation layer on top of stateful streams (toSignal(stream.value$)).

Stores solve a different problem: shared mutable state. I deliberately made Stateful Observable without a write path. A value changes only because an input went through the loader. My premise is that a frontend owns no source of truth except user input, and everything else is a projection of an API. If your problem really needs many writers patching shared state, a store is the right tool. A stateful observable isn't.

Looks like a resource, doesn't it?

Yes and no. A resource is fine in a component that projects a single data source: one read, owned by that component, with loading, error and reload built in. It starts to need workarounds when you combine several sources, or when the data is held in a shared service: a cache shared between sections, invalidation after a write, cancelling a read nobody waits for, dropping user data at logout. In the contest in part 2, the resources entry needed per-entity registries and a version counter for invalidation, and it still failed 14 scenarios.

A stateful observable is one solution that works the same way everywhere: in a component, in a shared service or token, and in a combination of both. The contest entry in part 2 used the same handle for all of them.

Not only Angular

The library started in Angular apps, but it depends only on RxJS. It has no framework code, no browser globals and no timers of its own. The Angular parts in my examples (toObservable, inject, the async pipe) are glue on the consumer side.

So it runs in Node.js too. My other project, langflower, is a local visual workflow tool: a node graph that runs agents, tools, checks and human gates on a project folder. Its runtime, compiler and node SDK use Stateful Observable under the hood. That's a good fit, because an agentic workflow is the same problem as a page full of data: a graph of steps where each step can be in progress, fail or succeed, where a failure should stay local, and where a retry should rerun only the part that needs it.

Limitations

  • It's young, but not new. Version 0.8.0, one maintainer, a small user base. It didn't appear overnight, though. The first version went to npm in October 2025, and 16 releases have followed since. The design grew out of earlier iterations described in the ADR (a wrapping operator, then a small store), and today it has a suite of 733 tests. It's also a thin layer over RxJS, so what you rely on underneath (switchMap, shareReplay, combineLatest) is mature.
  • There's no write path, by design. You can't patch cached data. Saves are requests whose result you show (through the input or a separate save stream). Optimistic UI is possible as an overlay you write yourself.
  • Two things to know about pipes. Both come with features plain RxJS doesn't have. Pending can't tell a value dropped by filter inside a pipe from a request still running, so the node stays pending; validation belongs on the input. And the stream survives an error, where plain RxJS would stop, but operator state such as scan starts over after it.
  • No runtime devtools yet. A prototype exists: an operator that sends every event to the Redux DevTools extension. It isn't shipped, because a proper integration has to be on in development builds and absent from production, and that switch ties it to each framework's build tools. The core stays framework-agnostic, so devtools would mean a separate package per framework. Until then, the graph topology makes tracing cheap: a log callback on a root traces every node derived from it, and nodes carry names and meta. If you'd use devtools, tell me in an issue: that decides whether the packages get built.
  • No time-based cache policy out of the box. A TTL or polling is composed from RxJS operators and reload().
  • Events are plain RxJS work. RxJS is good at managing events as it is: debounce, merges, sequences, time windows. The library doesn't replace that. It closes the gap that RxJS leaves for async data that can fail.

Recipes for people and agents

The library ships recipes, a quality-of-life guide and design decisions, written for both people and AI agents: where a source lives, how to invalidate the cached values of a subtree (for example on logout), how to batch a lookup, how to refresh what a write changed, and why the library works the way it does. In a check on the page from part 2, an agent given the recipes built a slice of it (a session, a batched lookup per row, a polled section, a write that refreshes another view) and followed the intended pattern on every point, with no steering.

Try it 

npm install @rx-evo/stateful-observable

import {
  statefulObservable,
  combineStatefulObservables,
} from "@rx-evo/stateful-observable";

const user$ = statefulObservable({
  input: userId$,
  loader: (id: number) => api.getUser(id),
  name: "user",
});

user$.subscribe({
  pending: (isLoading) => console.log("loading:", isLoading),
  next: (user) => console.log("user:", user),
  error: (error) => console.error("error:", error),
});
  • Source and docs: github.com/earthdmitriy/stateful-observable
  • npm: @rx-evo/stateful-observable
  • Recipes: docs/recipes.md
  • Quality-of-life guide: docs/QoL.md
  • Design decisions: docs/adr.md

Does it hold up on a real page? In part 2, I build one busy page four ways (plain RxJS, Stateful Observable, Angular signals with resources, NgRx SignalStore), judge all of them with the same test suite, and count the code.

If you've written tap(() => this.loading = true) more than once this year, try a stateful observable on one screen. If it saved you some plumbing, star the repo. If it didn't, open an issue and tell me why.

articles.title: Vercel said "Ready". Every route returned 500.
articles.description: Vercel said "Ready". My users got nothing.  Twelve seconds after I hit deploy, the dashboard showed...
articles.body_html:
Vercel said "Ready". My users got nothing.

Twelve seconds after I hit deploy, the dashboard showed "Deployed to Production" and "Ready". I turned off Deployment Protection, opened the URL — and every single route answered 500. Not one route. All of them. The root page. The health check. The API. FUNCTION_INVOCATION_FAILED, error rate 100%.

That is the worst kind of failure in software: the deploy is green and the service is dead. Nothing in the dashboard says "broken". Nothing is red. The production deployment says "Ready" while serving nothing at all.

And the cruelest part: everything had passed. 84 of 84 tests. The server answered 200 on every route from my own machine — including the legal and illegal example replays. The code was fine. The code was not the problem. The wiring between the code and the runtime was.

So I stopped re-reading my own code and did the one thing that actually finds this class of bug: I compared it with its working sibling. Wildcard 11 — same shape, same framework preset, same vercel.json, live and answering 200s. I diffed the two server files, and the difference was at the very bottom. Wildcard 11 ends by creating the server, exporting it as the default export, and listening only when run directly — with a comment that Vercel's Node runtime requires the default export to be a function or a server. Wildcard 12 ended differently: it exported a named buildServer function and never created a server instance at all. Locally that is fine — node server.js calls buildServer() and listens. On Vercel there was nothing to route through. The runtime tried to invoke a function that did not exist, on every request, and answered 500 for all of them.

The fix was 8 lines: create the server from buildServer(), export it as default, and listen on that same instance when run directly. Tests: 84 of 84. Local checks: all 200s, legal replay legal, illegal replay illegal. Push, Vercel redeployed automatically, and I verified live twice: root 200, health 200, examples 200 with 16 examples, legal example replayed legal 5-for-5, illegal example rejected naming exactly one rule, A04-steal-target-adjacent.

By the numbers: 12 seconds to deploy. 100% error rate. 84 of 84 tests green. 8 lines to fix. 15 seconds between a lying check and a true one — the first live check after the redeploy still showed 500, the second showed 200, because the old deployment was still serving while the new one rolled out. Verify twice, fifteen seconds apart. The first check can lie.

Three lessons, all cheap to learn here and expensive anywhere else:

First — a green deploy is not a live service. "Ready" describes the deployment, not the app. Check the real routes after every deploy. The health endpoint exists precisely for this, and it was the first thing that failed.

Second — when code works locally and dies in production, diff against a working sibling before re-reading your own code. My own file looked correct. The difference only showed up next to the one that worked.

Third — the error message told the truth. FUNCTION_INVOCATION_FAILED does not mean the function crashed. It means the runtime could not invoke anything. There was no function to invoke. Read the error literally before reaching for a deeper theory.

Season 01 ends tonight. I am sitting at rank 13 with 550.1 points, 44 verified-correct gatekeeper decisions and 2 timeouts. Eleven wildcard demos are live — the latest one, the subject of this story, at agentgames-wildcard-demo-12.vercel.app. This one was dead on arrival and fixed in 8 lines. The deploy said Ready, the service said 500, and the difference was a default export.

Built for #AgentGames — @ZKVProtocol.

articles.description: Office.js has no changelog. Microsoft ships new builds to its CDN edge by edge, and the first sign of...
articles.body_html:
Office.js has no changelog. Microsoft ships new builds to its CDN edge by edge, and the first sign of a change is usually an add-in that behaves differently. I run silentship, which samples the Office.js CDN every 10 minutes and compares the public API surface of each new build with the previous one. This week there were two things worth writing up: a new build, and a quiet change to the advice about which CDN URL to use.

1. Office.js 16.0.20710: what changed

Build 16.0.20710.15050 finished rolling out on 20 November on both the production and beta tracks. No documented API was removed and no signature changed. Two changes matter to add-in developers.

allowTextToOverflow on Excel chart data labels, ahead of the docs

All six Excel host files (Windows, Mac, web, iOS, Android, WinRT) now have allowTextToOverflow on both Excel.ChartDataLabel and Excel.ChartDataLabels. It is a regular scalar property: getter, setter, loadable, included in set() and toJSON().

It is not documented yet, and neither @types/office-js (1.0.617) nor @types/office-js-preview (1.0.738) knows about it, so TypeScript won't either. In the code it sits behind a requirement check for version 1.20, the same way the data-label properties from ExcelApi 1.19 (such as geometricShapeType) sit behind "1.19". So it most likely belongs to ExcelApi 1.20.

From the name, it probably controls whether label text may run outside its shape. That's a guess until Microsoft documents it. Until then, don't ship code that depends on it. If you want to experiment, check for it first:

const canTry =
  Office.context.requirements.isSetSupported("ExcelApi", "1.20") &&
  "allowTextToOverflow" in Excel.ChartDataLabel.prototype;

Office.ribbon.requestUpdate got a new body

This one is easy to miss. Office.ribbon.requestUpdate (RibbonApi 1.1) is how add-ins show and update contextual tabs and enable or disable ribbon buttons. In this build its implementation changed while its signature stayed the same.

Same signature means your code still compiles and calls it the same way. A new body means the behaviour may differ. If your add-in uses contextual tabs or toggles button states, test them on this build.

(A side note on tooling: my own classifier first labelled this method "undocumented". The type definitions describe it on the Office.Ribbon interface, but at runtime it lives on the Office.ribbon object, and the catalogue didn't connect the two. It does now, for Office.ribbon, Office.context.* and other APIs you reach through an object rather than a class.)

Noise you can ignore

set() and toJSON() on both data-label classes also changed. I compared the old and new versions of those methods, and the only difference is one more name in the list of properties they handle. These methods are generated and list every property of their class, so they change whenever a property is added or removed. They don't do anything new. silentship now treats this kind of change as a side effect of the new member and rates it low.

Everything else was in undocumented internals that add-ins shouldn't touch:

Change Member
added Office.api, OfficeCore.ApiVersionService, OfficeExtension.MarkOfAi
removed launchAgent from Office.ExtensionLifeCycle and OfficeCore.ExtensionLifeCycle, Excel.ActionCellValueType
new body OfficeCore.DimeApi.launch, Excel.CustomFunctionProxy

How the rollout went

Production Beta
First seen 16 Nov, 22:30 UTC 16 Nov, 22:30 UTC
Complete on appsforoffice 20 Nov, 10:10 UTC 20 Nov, 06:50 UTC
Complete on OneCDN 20 Nov, 10:50 UTC 20 Nov, 11:40 UTC

It took about three and a half days from the first sighting to every sampled edge. It also overlapped with the previous build: 16.0.20710 appeared before 16.0.20702 had finished rolling out, and some edges went straight from 16.0.20626 to 16.0.20710. For a few days, the same add-in could load any of three builds, depending on which edge answered. If a user reports a bug you can't reproduce during a week like this, that may be why.

2. Microsoft quietly went back to appsforoffice.microsoft.com

From September to November 2026, Microsoft's docs called appsforoffice.microsoft.com a legacy endpoint and recommended a new one:

appsforoffice OneCDN
Release appsforoffice.microsoft.com/lib/1/hosted/office.js officeapis.public.onecdn.static.microsoft/1/office.js
Preview appsforoffice.microsoft.com/lib/beta/hosted/office.js officeapis.public.onecdn.static.microsoft/beta/office.js

On 19 November Microsoft reverted its docs. They now point at appsforoffice.microsoft.com everywhere again. The new endpoint and the migration steps are gone, and no reason was given.

What the new endpoint actually changed

The docs said the new endpoint "enables additional secure defaults" but never said which. When I compared the two endpoints (first on 16.0.20606, again on 16.0.20710):

  • Same build on both.
  • Host files are byte-identical. excel-win32-16.01.js, word-win32-16.01.js and the rest have the same SHA-256. Every Office API you call comes from the same code.
  • Only the loader office.js differs, by two lines at the top: 
isOsfSecurityDefaultsEnabled = true;
osfLoadMsAjax = false;

With these set, the loader doesn't load MicrosoftAjax and creates a Trusted Types policy named officejs. The host files also look up function commands (ExecuteFunction in the manifest) only among handlers registered with Office.actions.associate(...), with no fallback to a global function of the same name on window.

What it means for you now

  • You never moved: nothing to do. appsforoffice.microsoft.com is the documented URL again.
  • You moved to OneCDN: your add-in keeps working. The endpoint hasn't changed and still serves the same files. It's just on a URL the docs no longer mention. Moving back is a one-line change, and since the API code is identical, the only difference you'd notice is the two loader defaults above.

  • Everyone: the defaults the new endpoint turned on are still worth testing against, because nothing stops them from appearing in the appsforoffice loader one day. The things that break are:

    • code (yours or a dependency's) that relies on MicrosoftAjax globals without knowing it: Sys.*, Type.registerNamespace, Function.createDelegate, $create. Search your bundle, not just your source: 
    grep -rnE '\bSys\.|Type\.registerNamespace|Function\.createDelegate|\$create\(' dist/
    • function commands defined only as plain globals. Register them with Office.actions.associate("onAction", onAction).
    • a strict CSP with Trusted Types, which needs to allow the officejs policy.

You can try the same defaults on the documented URL in a test build by setting the globals yourself before the loader:

<script>
  var isOsfSecurityDefaultsEnabled = true;
  var osfLoadMsAjax = false;
</script>
<script src="https://appsforoffice.microsoft.com/lib/1/hosted/office.js"></script>

I read this from the code and haven't tested it in every host, so use it to find hidden dependencies in a test build, not as a production setting. The full write-up covers the data-enable-trusted-types and data-use-associated-actions-only attributes, which have a gotcha: "true" turns the feature off, and only "1" turns it on.

Why I keep watching this

Both of this week's stories have the same shape: something changed on the CDN, or in what the docs say about it, and nothing announced it. An undocumented property showed up in production before the types knew about it. A documented ribbon method changed inside. A recommended endpoint stopped being recommended two months after it was introduced.

silentship watches both endpoints and both tracks and alerts by email or Slack when a build changes an API you use. You can set a watchlist and a minimum severity, so you only hear about what affects your add-in. A change to either loader flag on either endpoint counts as high.

Full data for this build: production rollout · beta rollout · Excel.ChartDataLabel · RSS
