articles.title: Why I Build Micro-Utilities as Zero-Backend Browser Tools on Cloudflare Workers (3 Real Examples)
articles.description: Most single-purpose utility websites fail for a boring reason: they treat a 60-line client-side...
articles.body_html:
Most single-purpose utility websites fail for a boring reason: they treat a 60-line client-side calculation like an enterprise SaaS app. They ask for an email address before showing an answer, upload a user's photo to an S3 bucket just to downsample pixels, or hardcode a scraped lookup table with no source provenance.

Over the past few months I have been building and refining a small portfolio of narrow craft, puzzle, and reference tools deployed on Cloudflare Workers and Pages. My self-imposed constraint for every tool is simple: zero login wall, zero server-side user data storage, deterministic browser-local execution, and clean open-source core logic.

Here are three concrete engineering problems that came up across three very different niches—and the tiny zero-dependency JavaScript/JSON modules I open-sourced for each.

1. Solving Word Ladders in Milliseconds Without an O(N^2) Graph

A word ladder connects two equal-length words (like COLD to WARM) by changing strictly one letter per step, where every intermediate rung must be a real English word.

The textbook mistake when building a browser solver is precomputing pairwise Hamming distances across the dictionary. On a 4,000-word dictionary, comparing every word pair takes ~8 million string comparisons on every page load or forces you to ship a megabyte of prebuilt adjacency lists.

Instead, you can group dictionary words into single-letter wildcard buckets in O(N * L) time (cold maps into *old, c*ld, co*d, col*), then run standard Breadth-First Search (BFS) over the buckets while deleting each visited bucket so it is never scanned twice:

function buildPatternBuckets(words) {
  const patterns = new Map();
  for (const word of words) {
    for (let i = 0; i < word.length; i += 1) {
      const pattern = `${word.slice(0, i)}*${word.slice(i + 1)}`;
      const bucket = patterns.get(pattern);
      if (bucket) bucket.push(word);
      else patterns.set(pattern, [word]);
    }
  }
  return patterns;
}

In a classroom setting there is a second subtle problem: an unfiltered Scrabble dictionary produces mathematically shortest paths through obscure words like CWM or VOLE that confuse 3rd-grade students. Separating a hand-reviewed everyday word list (plus a tiny 3-letter CVC phonics list) from the BFS engine makes the solver genuinely useful for teachers.

  • Interactive tools: Word Ladder Solver · Daily Word Ladder Practice · Winter Classroom Word Ladders
  • Open-source library & 46 verified puzzles (MIT): huangyifei1216/word-ladder-solver-js

2. Modeling Messy Real-World Standards: Why a US "G-6" Crochet Hook Breaks Naive Maps

Reference tables look deceptively simple until you model real physical standards.

When building CrochetSize.com, I assumed a crochet hook conversion chart was a trivial { "H-8": 5.0 } dictionary. It isn't. Across major yarn-craft manufacturers:

  1. US G-6 is manufactured at 4.0 mm by some brands and 4.25 mm by others.
  2. US 7 has a number label (4.5 mm) with no letter, sitting awkwardly between G-6 and H-8.
  3. 12.75 mm appears in standard tables with no US crochet-hook letter at all (null).
  4. Large hooks (M/N-13, N/P-15, P/Q, T/U/X) use slash-merged labels that differ by brand.

If you key your JSON object by US label and store a single float, you silently lie to users who own a 4.25 mm G-6 hook. Modeling metric diameter (metricMm) as an array ([4, 4.25]), explicitly flagging variation: true, and recording exact upstream revision provenance (adapted from Wikipedia rev. 1360857183 under CC BY-SA 4.0) keeps both the JSON/CSV exports and the UI honest:

{
  "id": "wikipedia-row-06",
  "metricMm": [4, 4.25],
  "metricDisplay": "4 or 4.25",
  "usLabel": "G-6",
  "variation": true,
  "checkNote": "May be 4 or 4.25 mm depending on the brand."
}
  • Interactive charts & hook guides: Crochet Hook Sizes in mm · Yarn Weight to Hook Size Chart (CYC 0–7) · G-6 Hook Guide
  • Open dataset (JSON + CSV + JS helper, CC BY-SA 4.0): huangyifei1216/crochet-hook-sizes-data

3. Keeping Image & Craft Math 100% Browser-Local

The third utility, Thread & Grid, converts photos or text into printable cross stitch and Perler bead charts and calculates fabric cut dimensions.

Historically, "photo to cross stitch" sites uploaded your family photo to a PHP or Python backend, queued a job, and emailed a PDF ten minutes later. Today, HTML5 Canvas + a lightweight color quantization pass + pure ESM sizing math can handle all of it locally in the browser tab in under 200 ms.

Even the fabric sizing calculation has an edge case beginners get wrong constantly: stitching "over 2" threads on Evenweave or Linen. A 28-count Evenweave stitched over 2 threads has the exact same effective density (14 stitches/inch) as 14-count Aida stitched over 1—and forgetting the 2 x margin framing border on both width and height ruins expensive linen cuts.

export function calculateCrossStitchSize({
  stitchesWide,
  stitchesHigh,
  fabricCount,
  overTwo = false,
  marginInches = 3,
}) {
  const stitchesPerInch = overTwo ? fabricCount / 2 : fabricCount;
  const designWidthIn = stitchesWide / stitchesPerInch;
  const designHeightIn = stitchesHigh / stitchesPerInch;
  return {
    stitchesPerInch,
    designWidthIn,
    designHeightIn,
    cutWidthIn: designWidthIn + marginInches * 2,
    cutHeightIn: designHeightIn + marginInches * 2,
  };
}
  • Interactive tools: Cross Stitch Size Calculator · Photo to Cross Stitch Maker · Perler Bead Pattern Generator
  • Open-source math module (MIT): huangyifei1216/cross-stitch-size-calculator-js

Why Edge + Browser-Local Wins for Micro-Tools

Running static assets and lightweight SSR pages on Cloudflare Workers/Pages while executing all math, search, and image quantization on the user's device gives four immediate advantages:

  1. Zero marginal compute bill when a seasonal page spikes (for example, crochet queries surge every December, and classroom puzzles surge on Monday mornings).
  2. Instant privacy compliance — no user images, no PII, no auth databases to breach.
  3. Composable open-source modules — every algorithm or dataset can be tested with node --test and published cleanly on GitHub for other developers to reuse.
  4. Faster perceived UX — zero spinner round-trips on every slider or input change.

If you're building niche web utilities, try deleting the backend first. You might be surprised how much of your product is cleaner, faster, and cheaper when it lives in 100 lines of pure ESM.

articles.title: Can the Visitor's Device Draw This Emoji? I Checked All 3,963 in Chrome With Four Different Fonts
articles.description: When you put an emoji on a web page as text, your server doesn't draw it. The visitor's device does,...
articles.body_html:
When you put an emoji on a web page as text, your server doesn't draw it. The visitor's device does, with whatever emoji font it has. A phone that hasn't been updated for a few years draws a newer emoji as an empty box, or as two older emoji side by side. Nobody gets an error message.

That matters most in two places. One is emoji pickers: if yours offers 🫫 cracking face (new in Emoji 18.0) to someone whose device can't draw it, they pick a box. The other is emoji favicons. An SVG favicon that contains the emoji as text is drawn by the visitor's font too. You can see this in the SVG that EmojiFavicons returns for /rocket. It's a small <text> element with 🚀 in it, so every browser draws its own rocket.

Browsers have no "can you draw this?" API, so the usual trick is to draw the emoji on a hidden canvas and inspect the pixels. I wanted to know how well that trick works and what it costs. On 21 November 2026, I ran three variants against all 3,963 fully-qualified emoji in Unicode's emoji-test.txt (Emoji 18.0), with four different font setups.

The setup

  • Browser: Chrome 156, headless, on a Linux VM (8 vCPU Xeon). I didn't test Firefox, Safari, Windows, macOS or phones. More on that at the end.
  • Emoji list: the 3,963 lines marked fully-qualified in emoji-test.txt, each with the Emoji version it arrived in.
  • Four font setups, switched with fontconfig so Chrome could only see the fonts I gave it:
    1. Today: Noto Color Emoji 2.051 (the current Debian package). It covers Emoji 17.0.
    2. Old: Noto Color Emoji 2.034 from November 2021 (Emoji 14.0), downloaded from the noto-emoji releases.
    3. Older: a Noto Color Emoji build from April 2020, tagged for Unicode 12.1.
    4. No emoji font: only DejaVu, which has black-and-white versions of some symbols.

Every check ran three times per setup. I report the median time.

Three ways to ask the canvas

All three draw the emoji at 32 px on a small canvas with the same font stack your page uses, then look at the result.

const ctx = document.createElement('canvas').getContext('2d', { willReadFrequently: true });
ctx.canvas.width = ctx.canvas.height = 40;
ctx.font = '32px "Noto Color Emoji", "Apple Color Emoji", "Segoe UI Emoji", sans-serif';
ctx.textBaseline = 'top';

function pixels(e) {
  ctx.clearRect(0, 0, 40, 40);
  ctx.fillText(e, 0, 0);
  return ctx.getImageData(0, 0, 40, 40).data;
}
function hasColour(d) {                 // any pixel that isn't black, white or grey
  for (let i = 0; i < d.length; i += 4)
    if (d[i + 3] && Math.max(d[i], d[i + 1], d[i + 2]) - Math.min(d[i], d[i + 1], d[i + 2]) > 30) return true;
  return false;
}
const hash = (d) => d.reduce((h, v) => (h * 31 + v) | 0, 0);
const TOFU = hash(pixels('\u{10FFFD}'));          // a code point no font draws: the "missing glyph" box
const ONE = ctx.measureText('\u{1F600}').width;   // width of one emoji
  • A. Colour test. If any pixel is coloured, assume the emoji was drawn. This is the version you'll find most often.
  • B. Colour + one glyph. Same, but also require the text to be about one emoji wide (measureText(e).width <= ONE * 1.4). When a font doesn't know a ZWJ sequence such as 🐦‍🔥 phoenix, it draws the parts, 🐦 and 🔥, so the result is twice as wide.
  • C. Not the box + one glyph. Don't look at colour at all. Compare the pixels with the missing-glyph box, and check the width.

What each check said

"Should draw" is the number of emoji up to the font's Emoji version. The 2020 build turned out to be incomplete (more below), so I left that cell empty.

Font setup Should draw A: colour B: colour + one glyph C: not the box + one glyph C: time for all 3,963
Noto 2.051 (today) 3,944 3,862 3,862 3,944 445 ms
Noto 2.034 (Emoji 14.0) 3,624 3,850 3,590 3,640 359 ms
Noto, April 2020 n/a 3,632 2,968 3,062 290 ms
No emoji font 0 0 0 1,275 41 ms

A and B took roughly the same time as C (270–360 ms with a font, 30–50 ms without).

On today's font, C was exact: it found all 3,944 emoji up to 17.0 and rejected all 19 from Emoji 18.0, which this font doesn't have yet. The others went wrong in instructive ways.

The colour test hides emoji that have no colour. With today's font, A rejected 82 emoji that drew perfectly well: 🖤 black heart, 🤍 white heart, 🩶 grey heart, 💬 speech balloon, 💭 thought balloon, 🕳️ hole, and, with the older fonts, the grey 🐺 wolf and 🦝 raccoon. Their pixels are all black, white or grey, so they look like a missing glyph to a colour test.

The colour test lets broken sequences through. With the 2021 font, A said yes to 276 emoji the font doesn't have, and 265 of them were ZWJ sequences that fell apart into coloured pieces. 🐦‍🔥 phoenix drew as a bird next to a flame. 🙂‍↔️ head shaking horizontally drew as two separate pieces. Both pieces are coloured, so a pixel test passes. Only the width check catches it, which is why B and C agree here and A doesn't.

"Not the box" is fooled by a black-and-white font. With no emoji font installed, C said yes to 1,275 emoji, because DejaVu has plain line drawings for many of them, including 😀. That's a symbol, not the emoji your design expects. The fix is one extra test up front: if 😀 has no colour, there's no emoji font, so treat everything as not drawable.

One more trap: flags. 🇨🇶 flag: Sark (Emoji 16.0) passed every test on both old fonts. It was one glyph, coloured, and not the box. In a screenshot it was Noto's placeholder, a white flag with a question mark. Comparing against a made-up flag, 🇽🇽, catches that.

The check I'd ship

Putting the lessons together:

const HAS_EMOJI_FONT = hasColour(pixels('\u{1F600}'));
const UNKNOWN_FLAG = hash(pixels('\u{1F1FD}\u{1F1FD}'));   // "XX" isn't a country

function canDraw(e) {
  if (!HAS_EMOJI_FONT) return false;
  if (ctx.measureText(e).width > ONE * 1.4) return false;   // fell apart into pieces
  const h = hash(pixels(e));
  return h !== TOFU && h !== UNKNOWN_FLAG;
}

Run on all 3,963 emoji, it took 290–460 ms per run on this machine (median per font setup: 459, 318 and 291 ms, and next to nothing with no emoji font, where it stops at the first line). That's fine once, in the background, but it's too slow to do every time the picker opens, and a low-end phone will be slower than a server CPU (I didn't measure one).

The shortcut: one emoji per version

Most emoji fonts are updated one Emoji version at a time, so you can test a single new emoji from each version and assume the rest follow:

const SENTINELS = [[1, '😀'], [11, '🥭'], [12, '🦩'], [12.1, '🧑‍🦯'], [13, '🫕'], [13.1, '😶‍🌫️'],
  [14, '🫠'], [15, '🫨'], [15.1, '🐦‍🔥'], [16, '🫩'], [17, '🫪'], [18, '🫫']];
const maxVersion = () => SENTINELS.reduce((v, [ver, e]) => (canDraw(e) ? ver : v), 0);

That took about 1 ms. It picked 17, 14, 12 and 0 for the four setups, and it never showed an emoji that didn't draw. But it was too strict:

  • With the 2021 font it hid 15 emoji that drew fine, all skin-tone versions of 🤼 people wrestling. Unicode only listed those in Emoji 17.0, but this Noto font already drew them in 2021.
  • With the 2020 build it hid 51. That build fails the 12.1 sentinel, 🧑‍🦯 person with white cane: it draws a person and a separate cane. But it does draw 30 of the 168 Emoji 12.1 emoji, mostly couples with mixed skin tones such as 🧑🏻‍🤝‍🧑🏿, plus five skin-tone handshakes 🤝🏻 from Emoji 14.0 and the same 15 wrestlers. The 51st was ⚧️ transgender symbol, which DejaVu drew in black and white. canDraw() wrongly accepts that one too (more below).

Both: the sentinel first, then test only what's newer

The version check is right about everything it lets through. So use it for that part, and run canDraw() only on emoji newer than the version it found:

function drawableList(list) {               // list: [{ e: '🫠', v: 14 }, ...] from emoji-test.txt
  const v = maxVersion();
  return list.filter((x) => x.v <= v || canDraw(x.e));
}

In my runs this gave exactly the same answers as testing all 3,963 one by one, in every setup, in a fraction of the time:

Font setup Version found Emoji tested one by one Drawable Time (median)
Noto 2.051 17 19 3,944 1.9 ms
Noto 2.034 14 339 3,639 3.3 ms
Noto, April 2020 12 953 3,061 8.7 ms
No emoji font 0 3,963 (all fail fast) 0 0.3 ms

The numbers stay small even with the older fonts, because most unsupported emoji fail on the cheap width check before any pixels are read.

Two practical notes. Cache the result, for example in localStorage keyed by navigator.userAgent, and run the check again when the browser version changes. And draw with exactly the same font string as your picker. If the picker uses a web emoji font and the canvas uses the system one, you are testing the wrong font.

What to do with an emoji that can't be drawn

  • In a picker: hide it, or show it greyed out with a short note ("may not display on this device"). Hiding is simpler. Greying out is kinder when people share content across devices, because the person reading may have a newer phone than the person writing.
  • In a favicon: an SVG favicon with an emoji in a <text> element is drawn by the visitor's font, so the same check applies. If the emoji you want is newer than a lot of your visitors' devices, use a picture instead of text. EmojiFavicons' ?png option returns a pre-rendered image. /phoenix?png gave me a 72×72 PNG of 🐦‍🔥, and that doesn't depend on the visitor's font at all. Our earlier 5-minute favicon health check covers the other half: making sure the right files are served at all.
  • When you're choosing one: the FindUtils Emoji Finder searches by keyword and copies an emoji as a character, code point or ready-made favicon tag. Check the result on the oldest device you care about before it goes into a logo or a launch post.

What I didn't test

  • Other browsers and systems. Apple Color Emoji, Segoe UI Emoji on Windows and Samsung's font all have their own coverage and their own placeholder glyphs. Firefox and Safari may also render canvas text a little differently. The approach should carry over, but the 1.4× width margin and the colour threshold are tuned to what I saw in Chrome.
  • Real phones. The timings come from a VM. Relative costs (1 ms vs 300+ ms) matter more than the absolute numbers.
  • Symbols a text font can draw. One false yes was left in my runs: on the 2020 build, ⚧️ was drawn in black and white by DejaVu, and canDraw() accepted it, because it was one glyph and not the box. If that matters for your picker, keep a short list of symbol-like emoji and require colour for those, accepting that a few truly black-and-white emoji (🖤, 🕳️) then need an exception.
  • Fonts loaded as web fonts. If you ship your own emoji font with @font-face, check that it has loaded (document.fonts.ready) before you run the check.

Checklist

  1. Don't trust a colour-only test: it hides black, white and grey emoji and lets broken ZWJ sequences through.
  2. Check the width as well, so an emoji that falls apart into pieces counts as unsupported.
  3. Check for an emoji font first (😀 should have colour).
  4. Compare against a made-up flag to catch placeholder flags.
  5. Find the version with one emoji per release, then test only the newer emoji one by one.
  6. Cache the answer per browser version, and use the picker's own font string.

The test scripts are small: a list parser, one HTML page and a Playwright runner. If you want to try the favicon side first, the EmojiFavicons docs list the SVG and PNG options.

Need help with a project? The team behind FindUtils takes on freelance work on Upwork, including Flutter apps for iOS and Android built from your idea or design, down to details like an emoji picker that only offers what the device can draw.

articles.title: Find circular dependencies in a TypeScript project: madge, import/no-cycle and a graph view
articles.description: Run madge --circular, dependency-cruiser or ESLint import/no-cycle to find TypeScript cycles. Real repomix output, which cycles crash Node, and fixes.
articles.body_html:
TL;DR

  • To find circular dependencies in a TypeScript project, run npx madge --circular --extensions ts,tsx src/, dependency-cruiser with a no-circular rule, or ESLint's import/no-cycle.
  • On repomix the three tools reported 8 cycles, 15 errors and 12 errors, and all three dropped to 0 once type-only and lazy import() edges were ignored.
  • A TypeScript cycle breaks at runtime only when one module reads a value from the other at load time: top-level code, a class extends, a decorator, or a registry call that runs on import.
  • 48 of 52 TypeScript repos with 1,000+ GitHub stars (92%) have at least one circular import chain between files.

The tool runs are on repomix at commit 758c3d71; the cohort numbers come from repowise's index of 195 public repos with 1,000+ GitHub stars (November 2026).

I ran three circular dependency checkers on the same TypeScript repo and got three different answers: 8 cycles, 15 errors and 12 errors. All three were pointing at the same two groups of files (15 files in all, 12 of them for ESLint). And when I told each tool to ignore imports that never run at load time, all three dropped to zero.

That gap is the whole story of circular dependencies in TypeScript. Most of them are harmless, a few crash Node on startup, and the tools count very different things. Below: when a cycle actually breaks (with repros you can run), how to find cycles with madge, dependency-cruiser and ESLint's import/no-cycle on a real project, why their numbers differ, and how to keep new ones out in CI.

How common are circular dependencies in TypeScript projects?

In a set of 195 public repositories with 1,000+ GitHub stars, 48 of the 52 TypeScript repos (92%) have at least one circular import chain between files. In the median TypeScript repo, 6.4% of production files sit inside one. Across all 195 repos the numbers are 89% and 9.2%. These are file-level chains in popular, working projects, which is the first hint that a cycle on its own is not a bug.

When does a circular dependency break at runtime?

Here are two files that import each other. config.ts exports defaults and logs a line. logger.ts reads the log level from the defaults when it loads.

// config.ts
import { log } from "./logger.ts";

export const defaults = { logLevel: "info", retries: 3 };

log("config loaded");

// logger.ts
import { defaults } from "./config.ts";

const level = defaults.logLevel;

export function log(msg: string) {
  console.log(`[${level}] ${msg}`);
}

// main.ts
import { defaults } from "./config.ts";

console.log("retries:", defaults.retries);

With "type": "module" in package.json, Node 22.19 runs .ts files directly (it strips the types), so no build step:

$ node main.ts
./logger.ts:3
const level = defaults.logLevel;
              ^

ReferenceError: Cannot access 'defaults' before initialization
    at ./logger.ts:3:15
    at ModuleJob.run (node:internal/modules/esm/module_job:345:25)
...

The order of events:

  1. main.ts imports config.ts. Before running it, Node follows its imports and finds logger.ts.
  2. logger.ts imports config.ts, which is already in progress, so Node does not go back. It runs logger.ts first.
  3. logger.ts line 3 reads defaults. In ES modules an import is a live binding to the exporter's variable, and that variable is a const that config.ts has not reached yet. It sits in the temporal dead zone, hence Cannot access 'defaults' before initialization.

Now move the read into the function:

// logger.ts
import { defaults } from "./config.ts";

export function log(msg: string) {
  console.log(`[${defaults.logLevel}] ${msg}`);
}

$ node main.ts
[info] config loaded
retries: 3

Same cycle, no error. By the time anyone calls log(), config.ts has assigned defaults, and the live binding sees the value. This is why most cycles in real projects never cause trouble: the import is only used inside functions that run later.

The CommonJS version fails differently

If your TypeScript compiles to CommonJS, the same two files fail with a different message. I compiled them with tsc --module commonjs --target es2022:

// out/logger.js (tsc output)
const config_1 = require("./config");
const level = config_1.defaults.logLevel;

$ node out/main.js
out/logger.js:5
const level = config_1.defaults.logLevel;
                                ^

TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'logLevel')

require("./config") returns the half-filled exports object of a module that is still running, so defaults is undefined. There is no TDZ in CommonJS, just a missing property. If you have ever seen a TypeError: x is not a function that only happens when files load in a certain order, this is a common cause.

Classes are the strict case, and import order decides

A class with extends needs its base class at the moment the class statement runs. Deferring the read into a function does not help, because the class statement runs at load time.

// shape.ts
import { Circle } from "./circle.ts";

export class Shape {
  area(): number {
    return 0;
  }

  static unit(): Shape {
    return new Circle(1);
  }
}

// circle.ts
import { Shape } from "./shape.ts";

export class Circle extends Shape {
  r: number;

  constructor(r: number) {
    super();
    this.r = r;
  }

  area(): number {
    return Math.PI * this.r ** 2;
  }
}

Two entry points that differ in one import line:

// a.ts
import { Shape } from "./shape.ts";

console.log(Shape.unit().area());

// b.ts
import { Circle } from "./circle.ts";
import { Shape } from "./shape.ts";

console.log(Shape.unit().area());

$ node a.ts
./circle.ts:3
export class Circle extends Shape {
                            ^

ReferenceError: Cannot access 'Shape' before initialization
...

$ node b.ts
3.141592653589793

b.ts works because circle.ts is entered first, so shape.ts finishes before class Circle extends Shape runs. a.ts enters from the other side and fails. The CommonJS build of a.ts fails with TypeError: Class extends value undefined is not a constructor or null. This is the cycle that bites people after an "unrelated" refactor or an import sort: nothing in the two class files changed, only which one got imported first.

So the short rule: a cycle breaks when one module reads a value from the other at load time. That means top-level code, a class extends, a decorator, or a registry call that runs on import. Reads inside functions that run later are fine. Type-only imports never run at all.

How do you find circular dependencies in a real TypeScript project?

I used repomix at commit 758c3d71 (8 November 2026): 147 TypeScript files in src/, ES modules with .js import specifiers, and verbatimModuleSyntax on in its tsconfig. Tool versions: madge 8.0.0, dependency-cruiser 18.7.2, ESLint 9.39.5 with eslint-plugin-import 2.32.0, Node 22.19.

One thing on safety first. Some JS tools load the project's own config files, which are code. For all three tools below, I kept the config in a folder outside the clone and pointed the tool at it, so nothing from the repo was executed. That is a good habit for any repo you did not write.

madge

madge parses imports and needs no config.

npx madge --circular --extensions ts,tsx src/

Processed 147 files (3.1s) (2 warnings)

✖ Found 8 circular dependencies!

1) core/packager.ts > core/skill/packSkill.ts
2) core/skill/packSkill.ts > core/skill/writeSkillOutput.ts
3) cli/actions/mcpAction.ts > mcp/mcpServer.ts > mcp/tools/attachPackedOutputTool.ts > mcp/tools/mcpToolRuntime.ts > cli/cliRun.ts
4) mcp/mcpServer.ts > mcp/tools/fileSystemReadDirectoryTool.ts
5) mcp/mcpServer.ts > mcp/tools/fileSystemReadFileTool.ts
6) mcp/mcpServer.ts > mcp/tools/grepRepomixOutputTool.ts
7) mcp/mcpServer.ts > mcp/tools/packCodebaseTool.ts
8) mcp/mcpServer.ts > mcp/tools/readRepomixOutputTool.ts

It exits with status 1, so it works as a CI gate as is. The 2 warnings are two gpt-tokenizer subpath imports it could not resolve (--warning lists them). If your project uses tsconfig paths aliases like @/lib/x, add --ts-config tsconfig.json, or those edges are silently missing from the graph.

Now look at where those cycles close. Every one of the 2-file loops goes back through an import type:

// src/mcp/tools/fileSystemReadDirectoryTool.ts
import type { McpServerConfig } from '../mcpServer.js';

// src/core/skill/packSkill.ts
import type { PackOptions, PackResult } from '../packager.js';

import type is erased at compile time. In the emitted JavaScript that edge does not exist, so it cannot cause any of the failures above. madge counts it by default. To make madge skip it, put a .madgerc in the directory you run from (madge reads it from the current directory and its parents):

{
  "detectiveOptions": {
    "ts": { "skipTypeImports": true },
    "tsx": { "skipTypeImports": true }
  }
}

✖ Found 1 circular dependency!

1) cli/actions/mcpAction.ts > mcp/mcpServer.ts > mcp/tools/attachPackedOutputTool.ts > mcp/tools/mcpToolRuntime.ts > cli/cliRun.ts

The one left closes in cliRun.ts, and it is deliberate:

// Each action is imported lazily so a run only loads the code path it takes.
const runCliDeps = {
  ...
  runMcpAction: async (...args: Parameters<typeof runMcpAction>) =>
    (await import('./actions/mcpAction.js')).runMcpAction(...args),

A dynamic import() inside a function runs when the function is called, long after every module has loaded. core/packager.ts does the same for packSkill with a comment explaining the reason (it saves about 25 ms of module loading). Add "skipAsyncImports": true next to skipTypeImports and madge prints:

✔ No circular dependency found!

So repomix has 8 circular dependencies by madge's default count and zero that can run into a half-loaded module.

dependency-cruiser

dependency-cruiser checks rules, and a cycle is one rule. With --no-config there are no rules, so it reports nothing:

$ npx depcruise src --no-config
✔ no dependency violations found (515 modules, 1236 dependencies cruised)

(It also followed imports into node_modules, hence 515 modules.) The rule goes in a config file. I wrote it as JSON, outside the clone, and passed it with --config:

{
  "forbidden": [
    {
      "name": "no-circular",
      "severity": "error",
      "from": {},
      "to": { "circular": true }
    }
  ],
  "options": {
    "doNotFollow": { "path": "node_modules" },
    "tsPreCompilationDeps": true
  }
}

tsPreCompilationDeps: true keeps type-only imports in the graph, which matches madge's default.

npx depcruise src --config ../cycle-rules/depcruise.json

  error no-circular: src/mcp/tools/readRepomixOutputTool.ts →
      src/mcp/tools/mcpToolRuntime.ts →
      src/cli/cliRun.ts →
      src/cli/actions/mcpAction.ts →
      src/mcp/mcpServer.ts →
      src/mcp/tools/readRepomixOutputTool.ts
...
  error no-circular: src/core/packager.ts →
      src/core/skill/packSkill.ts →
      src/core/packager.ts
...
x 15 dependency violations (15 errors, 0 warnings). 195 modules, 712 dependencies cruised.

The exit code was 15, one per error. To flag only cycles that matter at runtime, add viaOnly to the to block:

"to": {
  "circular": true,
  "viaOnly": { "dependencyTypesNot": ["type-only", "dynamic-import"] }
}

✔ no dependency violations found (195 modules, 712 dependencies cruised)

ESLint import/no-cycle

import/no-cycle from eslint-plugin-import puts the check in your linter and your editor. Here is the flat config (mine loads the two packages from a separate install folder, otherwise it is the same). I kept it outside the repo and ran ESLint with --no-config-lookup -c <path>, so it does not look for the project's own config:

// eslint.config.mjs
import tsParser from "@typescript-eslint/parser";
import importPlugin from "eslint-plugin-import";

export default [
  {
    files: ["src/**/*.ts", "src/**/*.tsx"],
    languageOptions: { parser: tsParser, ecmaVersion: "latest", sourceType: "module" },
    plugins: { import: importPlugin },
    settings: {
      "import/parsers": { "@typescript-eslint/parser": [".ts", ".tsx"] },
      "import/resolver": { typescript: { project: "./tsconfig.json" } },
    },
    rules: { "import/no-cycle": "error" },
  },
];

The typescript resolver comes from eslint-import-resolver-typescript. It maps ./mcpServer.js to mcpServer.ts and resolves paths aliases. Without it, most TypeScript imports do not resolve and the rule finds nothing.

npx eslint --no-config-lookup -c ../cycle-rules/eslint.config.mjs src

src/cli/actions/mcpAction.ts
  1:1  error  Dependency cycle via ./tools/attachPackedOutputTool.js:8=>./mcpToolRuntime.js:12=>../../cli/cliRun.js:6  import/no-cycle

src/cli/cliRun.ts
  374:12  error  Dependency cycle via ../../mcp/mcpServer.js:1=>./tools/attachPackedOutputTool.js:8=>./mcpToolRuntime.js:12  import/no-cycle
...
src/mcp/tools/readRepomixOutputTool.ts
  7:1  error  Dependency cycle via ../../cli/cliRun.js:6=>./actions/mcpAction.js:374=>../../mcp/mcpServer.js:1  import/no-cycle

✖ 12 problems (12 errors, 0 warnings)

ESLint reports on import statements, so you get one error per file that sits on a cycle, with the line of the import. Notice what is missing: the packager.ts / packSkill.ts loop. The rule already ignores import type, and that loop only closes through type imports. What it does count is the dynamic import() at cliRun.ts:374. The rule's option for that is allowUnsafeDynamicCyclicDependency:

rules: { "import/no-cycle": ["error", { allowUnsafeDynamicCyclicDependency: true }] },

With it, ESLint printed nothing and exited 0. On this repo ESLint took about 11 seconds, against 2 to 4 for the other two. On a big repo, the rule's maxDepth option limits how far it follows imports.

A graph view

The fourth view is the file graph itself. I indexed the same commit with repowise (repowise init --yes --no-prose --no-editor-setup) and grouped its stored import graph into strongly connected components: sets of files that can all reach each other.

cycle groups: 2 files in cycles: 15
12 ['src/cli/actions/mcpAction.ts', 'src/cli/cliRun.ts', 'src/mcp/mcpServer.ts', 'src/mcp/tools/attachPackedOutputTool.ts', ...]
3 ['src/core/packager.ts', 'src/core/skill/packSkill.ts', 'src/core/skill/writeSkillOutput.ts']

Dropping the edges marked type-only or deferred:

cycle groups: 0 files in cycles: 0

Two groups is the number I find easiest to act on. Every listed cycle, error and path above lives inside one of these two groups, and each group is one design decision: the MCP tools and the server that registers them, and the skill packer and the packager that loads it. In a graph UI you can open the 12-file group and see the loop as a picture, which is quicker to reason about than reading five-line paths. The JavaScript/TypeScript dependency graph guide has the commands for drawing the graph with each of these tools.

Why do madge, dependency-cruiser and ESLint report different counts?

Tool, default settings What it counts repomix Type-only and lazy imports dropped
madge --circular one path per loop it walks into 8 cycles 0
dependency-cruiser no-circular one violation per cycle it reports, written from the module where it starts 15 errors 0
ESLint import/no-cycle one error per import statement on a cycle 12 errors 0
Strongly connected components groups of files that all reach each other 2 groups, 15 files 0

Four things explain the gaps, and they apply to any repo:

  • Type-only imports. madge and dependency-cruiser (with tsPreCompilationDeps: true) count them. import/no-cycle skips them. That is the whole difference between ESLint's 12 and the other tools' 15 files here. TypeScript also drops imports used only as types even when you write a plain import { X }, unless verbatimModuleSyntax is on. With it on, as in repomix, you have to write import type, which also makes the intent visible to every tool.
  • Dynamic import(). madge, dependency-cruiser and ESLint all count it by default. It is safe at load time for the same reason a read inside a function is safe.
  • Path aliases and .js specifiers. A tool that cannot resolve @/lib/x or ./foo.js to a .ts file drops the edge without an error. If a tool finds far fewer cycles than another, check resolution first (--ts-config for madge, the typescript resolver for ESLint, tsConfig in dependency-cruiser's options).
  • Granularity. A path, an edge, an import statement and a group are different units. The 12-file group shows up as six madge paths, thirteen dependency-cruiser violations and twelve ESLint errors. madge's list also skips files: packRemoteRepositoryTool.ts and generateSkillTool.ts are in the group but in none of its eight paths. When the numbers disagree, count the files.

The madge vs dependency-cruiser comparison runs the same exercise on a much larger monorepo (Excalidraw), where the counts were 839 and 1,721 and the graph was three tangles.

How do you fix a circular dependency that breaks?

These are run against the config.ts / logger.ts repro from the top, in the order I would try them.

1. Make type-only imports explicit

If the import is only for types, write import type. It costs nothing, it is erased at compile time, and verbatimModuleSyntax (or the @typescript-eslint/consistent-type-imports rule) will make sure nobody forgets. It does not fix a runtime cycle, but it removes the noise so the real ones stand out.

2. Move the shared value into a leaf module

Both files needed defaults, so give it a file that imports nothing:

// defaults.ts
export const defaults = { logLevel: "info", retries: 3 };

// logger.ts
import { defaults } from "./defaults.ts";

const level = defaults.logLevel;

export function log(msg: string) {
  console.log(`[${level}] ${msg}`);
}

// config.ts
import { defaults } from "./defaults.ts";
import { log } from "./logger.ts";

export { defaults };

log("config loaded");

$ node main.ts
[info] config loaded
retries: 3

$ npx madge --circular --extensions ts fix-move
✔ No circular dependency found!

Even the top-level read in logger.ts is fine now, because defaults.ts always finishes first.

3. Invert the dependency

logger.ts does not need to know where its settings come from. Pass them in:

// logger.ts
export function createLogger(opts: { logLevel: string }) {
  return (msg: string) => console.log(`[${opts.logLevel}] ${msg}`);
}

// config.ts
import { createLogger } from "./logger.ts";

export const defaults = { logLevel: "info", retries: 3 };
export const log = createLogger(defaults);

log("config loaded");

logger.ts now imports nothing from the project, and madge reports no cycle. For the Shape / Circle case the same idea means Shape.unit() moves out of shape.ts into a small factory module that imports both, so the base class never imports its subclass.

4. Defer the read

Reading the value inside a function, or using await import() like repomix does, keeps the cycle but makes it safe. Fine for a local fix, and worth a comment saying why, as repomix does.

Barrel files

A barrel (index.ts that re-exports a folder) adds an edge from the barrel to every file in the folder. When a file inside the folder imports from its own barrel, you get a cycle through every sibling, which is where most of the huge cycle counts in TypeScript monorepos come from. The rule of thumb is to import siblings by path inside a package and use the barrel only from outside. Barrels get their own post next in this series, with numbers from the same 52 TypeScript repos.

How do you keep new circular dependencies out in CI?

Any of the three tools works as a gate. Pick based on where you want the error to show up.

# .github/workflows/cycles.yml (excerpt)
- run: npx madge --circular --extensions ts,tsx src/
# or
- run: npx depcruise src --config .dependency-cruiser.json
  • madge exits 1 on any cycle. With a .madgerc that sets skipTypeImports, it gates only cycles that exist in the emitted JavaScript.
  • dependency-cruiser exits with the number of errors and lets you write the rule as tightly as you want (viaOnly, or a path rule such as "src/core never imports src/cli", which stops cycles before they form). On a codebase that already has cycles, depcruise-baseline records today's violations and --ignore-known fails only on new ones. The comparison post above walks through that.
  • import/no-cycle is the one people see in their editor before they push, if ESLint already runs in your CI.

For a project starting at zero runtime cycles, like repomix with type-only and lazy imports excluded, the strict gate is cheap to adopt. For a project with hundreds, start with the baseline and the runtime-only rule, and shrink from there.

If you have cycles in Python or Go too, I covered Python's circular import errors and why Go repos barely have any in earlier posts.

Which of the three counts do you gate on in CI, and did it start at zero?

How I ran this

The cohort numbers come from 195 of the most-starred public repositories indexed on repowise (1,000+ GitHub stars each, 253,688 production source files, November 2026), counted on file-to-file imports between production files, each repo measured at its own latest index. The circular import section of the code health report has the per-language breakdown. Everything about repomix is from a fresh clone at 758c3d71 on 10 November 2026: madge 8.0.0, dependency-cruiser 18.7.2, ESLint 9.39.5 with eslint-plugin-import 2.32.0, @typescript-eslint/parser 8.72.2 and eslint-import-resolver-typescript 4.4.5, all installed in a separate folder, with every config file kept outside the clone. The graph view is repowise init --yes --no-prose --no-editor-setup on the same commit, followed by a strongly connected components pass over the stored import graph, once with every import edge and once without type-only and deferred edges. The repros ran on Node 22.19 (type stripping for .ts) and tsc 5.9.3 for the CommonJS builds.

FAQ

How do I find circular dependencies in TypeScript?
Run npx madge --circular --extensions ts,tsx src/ for a quick list, or add a no-circular rule to dependency-cruiser or import/no-cycle to ESLint if you want it in CI or in your editor. Set the tool to skip type-only and dynamic import() edges if you only care about cycles that can fail at runtime.

Does TypeScript allow circular imports?
Yes. The compiler does not reject two files that import each other, and Node runs them in both ES module and CommonJS output. A cycle only fails when one module reads a value from the other before that module has finished loading, which shows up as Cannot access 'x' before initialization in ES modules or an undefined value in CommonJS.

How do I fix a circular dependency in JavaScript?
Move the shared value into a leaf module that both files import, or invert the dependency so one side receives what it needs as an argument. Reading the import inside a function, or loading it with await import(), keeps the cycle but makes it safe at load time.

articles.title: Resurrecting HyperCard for the browser with Kiro — PhantomCard
articles.description: For Kiroween 2026 — AWS's spooky-season hackathon — I built PhantomCard: a resurrection of Apple's...
articles.body_html:
For Kiroween 2026 — AWS's spooky-season hackathon — I built PhantomCard: a resurrection of Apple's HyperCard that runs entirely in your browser. Stack of cards, buttons, fields, a working HyperTalk interpreter, System-7 monochrome chrome — no build step, no dependencies, just ES modules.

Try it live: https://till3005.github.io/phantomcard/ · Code: https://github.com/Till3005/phantomcard

Why HyperCard, and why "resurrection"?

Kiroween's Resurrection category asks you to bring dead technology back to life. HyperCard (1987) was the first mass-market hypermedia tool: a stack of "cards" holding buttons, fields and paint, scripted in HyperTalk — English-ish code like answer "Hello" with "OK" and go to next card. Entire generations learned programming by clicking around someone else's stack. Apple killed it in 2004, and browsers never quite replaced the magic of "open a stack, flip through cards, tweak a button's script."

PhantomCard resurrects that loop: you can flip through bundled demo stacks (a welcome tour, a séance deck, a haunted-house adventure), then hit Authoring mode and add a button, type its HyperTalk script, and watch it actually run.

How Kiro shaped the build

This is where Kiro stopped being a code generator and started being a collaborator:

  • Spec-driven development. Before a line of app code existed, we wrote the spec in .kiro/specs/phantomcard/: requirements (data model, HyperTalk grammar surface, interaction modes), a design doc, and a task list. When the agent drifted — proposing a React scaffold or a build step — the spec pulled it back. Every judgment call I made later traced to a spec decision, not a chat message.
  • Steering rules. .kiro/steering/ holds the rules Kiro worked under: zero build step, ES modules only, System-7 visual fidelity, no dependencies beyond lz-string. Those constraints are the reason the app loads instantly on GitHub Pages and the codebase stays readable end-to-end.
  • The HyperTalk interpreter — the hardest part — was co-written with Kiro CLI: a lexer, a recursive-descent parser, and an async interpreter with re-entrant send/dispatch semantics. Kiro wrote the grammar tests that caught edge cases (e.g. item idx of omens after put c + 1 into c).

What's in the box

  • 512×342 canvas-rendered cards with dissolve transitions (faithful to the original)
  • Buttons, fields, paint layers, custom Chrome menus and dialogs — all monochrome System 7
  • A real HyperTalk runtime: handlers, put/get/go/answer/ask, item/line chunks, the number of cards
  • URL-shareable stacks (state compressed into the link via lz-string)
  • Three demo stacks authored as HyperCard docs: Welcome, The Séance Deck, The Haunted House

What I'd do differently

The trickiest bug: a "dissolve" animation re-fired on every render, not just card changes — the fix was a one-line guard on the card id, found by watching a screen recording of the app in frame-by-frame. Retro-faithful doesn't mean stateless.

PhantomCard is MIT-licensed and in the running for Kiroween 2026's Resurrection category. If you grew up on HyperCard — or never got to — go flip a stack.
